t: terumot and ma'aserot etc.. Regarding the obligation of second tithe outside the Land of Israel see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 1:14.
even not in the presence of the Temple. At a time when the Temple does not exist (and see below, halachah 26 regarding the force of the obligation today).

and the prophets ordained that they apply even in the land of Shinar. In the period of the exile of the First Temple, when they were exiled mainly to Babylonia, the prophets ordained separating terumot and ma'aserot also in Babylonia (see Avot DeRabbi Natan ch. 20 and Commentary on the Mishnah, Yadayim 4:3).

and the early Sages ordained that they apply also in the land of Egypt etc.. In the Second Temple period the Sages ordained separation in additional lands because some of Israel went to settle in them (Rik"v, based on the Jerusalem Talmud).
and in the land of Ammon and Moab. East of the Jordan, and see the rulings and views.

the surroundings of the Land of Israel. Bordering the Land of Israel. And although they are nearer to it than Babylonia, their enactment was made later, because the main movement of Israel before then was between the Land of Israel and Babylonia (Radbaz).
the Land of Israel mentioned everywhere. With regard to commandments dependent on the Land and other matters.

even from the land that was given to Abraham. The borders of the land promised to Abraham our forefather (Genesis 15:19) are wider than the land actually conquered by those who came up from Egypt when they entered the Land (described in halachah 7). And even if an individual conquered an area of the promised land, this conquest does not obligate in the commandments dependent on the Land.
and for this reason Joshua divided etc.. See Joshua chapters 14-19 (especially 14:1, 19:51).
the lands that David conquered. See II Samuel chapters 8, 10.
and Achlav. It seems to be the city of Aleppo in Syria.

and not like outside the Land for all matters, such as Babylonia and Egypt. For although terumot and ma'aserot were ordained in Babylonia and Egypt (above, halachah 1), this is by force of an enactment and not because of conquest.
they left the category of outside the Land to be like the Land of Israel. For certain laws.
and they did not reach. The full level of the Land of Israel.
of the seven nations. The nations of Canaan.
and the lands that David conquered are called Syria. And its borders will be explained below, halachah 9.
and there are matters in which it is like the Land of Israel. See for example Hilchot Bikkurim 2:1, Hilchot Shabbat 6:1, 6:11.

and there are matters in which it is like outside the Land. See for example below 5:12, Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:2. There are also cases in which Syria has an intermediate status, see for example Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:3, Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 10:11-12.
and the Sabbatical year. See Hilchot Shemitah 4:27.
by the words of the Scribes. By the words of the Sages.
and it was sanctified with the first sanctification. Since the Land was conquered, holiness applied to it.
when the exiles went up. The ascent of Ezra, in which the Second Temple was built.

they sanctified it with a second sanctification that stands forever. Unlike the sanctity of those who came up from Egypt, which was nullified with the exile, this sanctity of those who came up from Babylon stands forever. The reason is that those who came up from Egypt applied the obligation of the commandments to the Land by conquest, and since the Land was taken from them, the conquest was nullified and the sanctity was nullified. By contrast, Ezra's returnees sanctified the Land by the possession they took of it, and it is valid forever (see Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:14-16). Later authorities discussed the nature of the difference between conquest and possession. Some wrote that conquest is done without the consent and recognition of the nations, as opposed to possession, which is done in an orderly and recognized manner (as the ascent of Ezra following Cyrus's declaration; see Tosafot Yom Tov, Eduyot 8:6, Responsa Sho'el UMeshiv, first edition, 1:124). In a different direction, some held that the difference is in the manner of sanctification, that the Babylonian returnees sanctified it by speech, in addition to dwelling on the land, and therefore it endures forever, whereas those who came up from Egypt did not sanctify it by speech (Radbaz; for further explanations see Even HaAzel on Hilchot Beit HaBechirah there, Chiddushim UBiurim to Hilchot Beit HaBechirah by the Lubavitcher Rebbe, sec. 16; Chevel Nachalato 6:34).

and they left those places... as they were and did not exempt them from terumot and ma'aserot. Although the sanctity of those places was nullified, the Sages established to treat them as they were before the exile, when those who came up from Egypt dwelt there and separated terumot and ma'aserot in them.

so that the poor may rely on them in the Sabbatical year. They ordained the law of terumot and ma'aserot in these places always and especially in the Sabbatical year, so that the poor of the Land of Israel, who do not receive gifts to the poor and tithes during the Sabbatical year, could receive them there (and see Rik"v, who had a different reading and explained differently). And regarding the status of these places with respect to the commandments of the Sabbatical year, see Hilchot Shemitah 4:26.
our holy teacher. Rabbi Yehudah HaNasi.
permitted Beit She'an. And exempted it entirely from terumot and ma'aserot, unlike the other places that those from Egypt conquered and those from Babylon did not.

and he was counted with Ashkelon and exempted it from the tithes. He permitted, with the agreement of the Sages who were counted with him, Ashkelon, which is also in the area of those who came up from Egypt.

what is the land that those who came up from Egypt took possession of?. It seems that here the Rambam means the common places that both those from Egypt and those from Babylon took possession of, and further on he will detail the differences between them (Yad Peshutah).
from Rekem, which is in the east of the Land of Israel. And is adjacent to the Dead Sea.
the Great Sea. The Mediterranean.

if he was walking from Acco to Chezib. Chezib is northeast of Acco (about 5 km north of Nahariya), and the area between them does not have a uniform status; rather what is east of the road between Acco and Chezib is presumed to be outside the Land until proven otherwise, and what is west of it is presumed to be the Land of Israel until proven otherwise.
impure because of the land of the nations. For the Sages decreed that what is outside the Land becomes impure with corpse impurity (Hilchot Tumat Met 11:1).
and whatever slopes etc.. Here the Rambam details the full borders of those who came up from Egypt.

and whatever slopes and descends from the mountains of Amanus inward. The northwestern border of the Land begins at the southern slopes of the Amanus mountain range (there are several opinions about the identification of this place, and in Responsa of the Rambam 127 he wrote that it is Mount "Baniyas," which is apparently in the coastal region of Syria).
and the islands in the sea. Islands in the sea.
one sees them as if a string were stretched over them etc.. See illustration.
the stream of Egypt. The southwestern border of the Land according to the Torah (Numbers 34:5), and the commentators disagree whether this is Wadi el-Arish or the Nile.

and this is its form. It is understood that the map the Rambam drew depicts the borders in general terms and is not careful about exact measures and locations. Nevertheless it is hard to understand several details that appear in it, and some of them even seem to contradict the Rambam's own words. The mountains of Amanus are marked on the map in the south of the Land, but it is clear that they in fact constitute the northern point of the border. The matter of the tongues of the sea and the islands is also not sufficiently clear. It should further be noted that from the drawing one might perhaps understand that east of the strip of the land of the nations beside the road between Acco and Chezib there is an additional area within the boundary of the Land of Israel.

from Chezib inward toward the east. It seems that the reference here is to the strip between Chezib and Acco mentioned above, halachah 7, and this strip, which is from Chezib and south ("from Chezib inward"), is part of the area of those who came up from Babylon (the phrase "toward the east" is difficult, since according to what was said above, halachah 7, it is precisely the western area between Acco and Chezib that is holy; see also the Rambam's drawing there).
and from Chezib outward to Amanah, which is Amanus. This is the northern area of those who came up from Egypt in which those who came up from Babylon did not take possession.
and to the river, which is the stream of Egypt. This is the southern area of those who came up from Egypt in which those who came up from Babylon did not take possession.
from the Land of Israel and below. From the Land of Israel northward. And in essence the area of Syria extends far to the northeast of the Land of Israel (see illustration on the next page).

but Acco is outside the Land like Ashkelon. It seems the intention is not outside the Land literally, but that these places are not included in the area of those who came up from Babylon (see Kesef Mishneh).

a gentile who bought land in the Land of Israel did not exempt it from the commandments, but it remains in its sanctity. And therefore it is in principle obligated in the commandments dependent on the Land (and see in the following halachot that there are cases in which produce that grew in a gentile's land is in practice exempt from terumot and ma'aserot).
and he brings bikkurim. See Hilchot Bikkurim 2:15.

and a gentile can acquire in Syria so as to exempt from tithes and from the Sabbatical year. And therefore produce that grew in Syria in land owned by a gentile is exempt from terumot and ma'aserot in every case.
as will be explained. Below, halachot 15-17.

if their work was completed in the hands of the gentile and the gentile smoothed them. "Completion of work" is the term for the final actions in the handling of the crop, and this is the stage at which the full obligation of terumot and ma'aserot applies to the produce (see Hilchot Ma'aser 3:1-2, that after completion of work it is forbidden to eat even a casual snack from produce intended for sale). For grain, the completion of work is the smoothing (merucha), which is the leveling and cleaning of the kernels after they were piled (there, halachah 5).

as it says "your grain" and not "the grain of a gentile". Grain is called "dagan" only after he made a pile of the kernels, and the Torah obligated grain in terumot and ma'aserot only if an Israelite made it into grain.
bought them. Acquired them.
they are obligated in everything by Torah law. Since a gentile's acquisition does not exempt from the tithes.

and terumat ma'aser, and sells it to the kohen, and first tithe, which is his. In the usual situation he gives the terumot and ma'aserot without payment, but here he is not obligated to give the kohen and the Levite the terumat ma'aser and the tithe. Therefore the terumat ma'aser, which is permitted for eating only to kohanim, he can sell to a kohen, and the tithe he can eat himself.
I came by the right of a man from whom you cannot take anything. For the gentile in whose possession the produce grew is not obligated in terumot and ma'aserot.

when you take from the children of Israel the tithe etc.. The verse deals with the Levites' obligation to separate terumat ma'aser from the tithe for the kohanim, and the Sages learned that if it grew in the gentile's possession he is not obligated to give the kohanim the terumat ma'aser, and therefore he can tell the Levite and kohen that since he bought it from the gentile he is exempt from giving to them. The same applies to the tithe (see Aruch HaShulchan par. 16, Derech Emunah and Yad Peshutah).

if before they came to the time of the tithes. The "time of the tithes" is the term for an early stage in the growth of the fruit at which the obligation of tithes begins (so that if one picks at this stage and wants to eat a fixed meal, he must tithe). For grain the time of the tithes is when it has grown a third (see Hilchot Ma'aser 2:3-5).
and if he sold them after they came to the time of the tithes. And after the Israelite bought them the fruit continued to grow in his possession.

he separates terumat ma'aser and the tithe and gives of them to the owners proportionally. Since the completion of work was in the Israelite's possession he is obligated to separate terumot and ma'aserot, but the obligation to give the terumat ma'aser and the tithe to the kohen and Levite is only in proportion to the share of the grain that grew in his possession, as will be explained shortly.
took sown grain from the gentile after it had reached a third. Which is the time of the tithes for grain (Hilchot Ma'aser 2:5).
he separates terumot and ma'aserot as we have explained. Above, halachah 11, since the completion of work was in the Israelite's hands.
and the gentile finished them, they are exempt from terumah and ma'aserot. By the law of a gentile's fruit whose work was completed by him (above, halachah 11).
they are obligated in everything by rabbinic law. The Sages obligated separating terumot and ma'aserot from them since they reached the time of the tithes while in an Israelite's possession.

and likewise a gentile who completed the work on an Israelite's produce. Even if the produce is still in the Israelite's possession and the gentile only performed the act of completing the work (Derech Emunah and Yad Peshutah).
they are not obligated in terumah and ma'aserot. Not even by rabbinic law.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 4.
a sharecropper. One who works another's field and takes a certain percentage of the crop, while the field is the owner's responsibility.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 10.
and likewise a leaseholder... is exempt from the tithes and from terumot. Although they take the field on their own responsibility
,. in Syria they are not considered owners of the field to be obligated in tithes.

the leaseholder, the sharecropper, and the renter. The leaseholder (chokher) pays the owner a fixed quantity of produce and not a proportional quantity. The sharecropper (mekabel) pays a certain percentage of the crop. And the renter (sokher) pays a fixed sum of money.
for it became obligated in the hands of an Israelite. For the field was in his possession both when it reached the time of the tithes and at the completion of work.

these are exempt, for I say that he bought from the market. Since the same fruit is found in the market and it may be that they are not from the fruit that grew in his possession, we are lenient out of doubt, since the obligation of separation in Syria is by rabbinic law.

even if they divided the field while standing. Although they divided the grain between them while it stood in the field and had not yet been harvested, we do not say that the half the gentile took is the exempt part from terumah and ma'aserot and the half the Israelite took is the obligated part, but half of the entire grain is obligated and half exempt since it grew in partnership.

needless to say if they divided the heap. That they divided the crop after it was harvested and piled in the field, in which case it is clear that one cannot regard each half of the grain as if it grew only in one of their shares.
tevel and chullin are mixed in every stalk of the gentile's share. For each unit is considered a mixture of grain that is obligated in tithes and grain that is exempt.
even though the gentile smoothed them. Although the gentile smoothed the portion he took, the Israelite's share mixed into it was not exempted thereby from the obligation of terumah and ma'aserot.
and their obligation is by rabbinic law as we have explained. Above, halachah 13, that an Israelite's grain that was smoothed by the gentile is obligated by the Sages' enactment.
in the Land of Israel, where the tithes are by Torah law. For grain in the Land of Israel is obligated essentially in terumah and ma'aserot by Torah law.

and in matters of Torah law there is no breirah. For in a matter concerning Torah law, one cannot rely on the fact that ultimately it will become clear what each one's portion is, and treat the half each one finally took as if it had been his share from the start; rather the entire grain is treated as mixed. The law of "breirah," i.e., the possibility of treating what became clear in the end as if it were so from the beginning, concerns many matters in halachah, and regarding it, it was established that in matters of Torah law we do not rely on retroactive clarification, whereas in matters of rabbinic law we may rely on it (see for example Hilchot Ma'aser 7:1, Hilchot Yom Tov 5:20).

but if they took a field in Syria... the gentile's share is exempt from everything. For in matters of rabbinic law we rely on breirah, even if they divided grain that had already been harvested, and we say that what the gentile took was his share from the start and is exempt from terumah and ma'aserot.
exempt from challah. By Torah law. However, the Sages ordained separating challah also outside the Land (see Hilchot Bikkurim 5:6-7).

and if they went out to Syria, they are obligated by rabbinic law. Since it is not like outside the Land (above, halachah 3), they are not considered produce that went out to outside the Land (see Radbaz).

and likewise produce from outside the Land that entered the Land is obligated in challah etc.. By Torah law. For the obligation of challah is determined by the place where the dough is kneaded (Radbaz).

and if they were fixed for tithing in the hands of an Israelite after they entered the Land, they are obligated in ma'aserot by rabbinic law. Although by Torah law they are exempt since they grew outside the Land and their law is determined by where they grew, if they were fixed for tithes in the Land they are obligated by rabbinic law (and Kesef Mishneh compared the law of challah to the law of terumah and ma'aserot, and wrote regarding all of them that just as kneading in the Land obligates challah by Torah law, so fixing for tithes obligates by Torah law. Only produce from outside the Land that was fixed for tithing outside the Land, after entering the Land, is obligated in ma'aserot by rabbinic law).
when the ship is touching the land. When the bottom of the ship touches and scrapes the ground, in which case what grows in it is considered to have grown in the soil of the Land of Israel.
everything follows the main part. The place where the roots are.
even if a solid rock separated between them etc.. Even if a continuous rock separates between them, and the roots cannot pass to the other side, each side of the tree is not treated separately.
tevel and chullin are mixed with one another. For each fruit is considered a mixture of tevel and chullin (Ritva, Bava Batra 27b).

a perforated pot containing a seed that had not taken root. If there is a hole at the bottom large enough for its roots to emerge and connect to the ground, but in practice they did not connect to the ground.
and its foliage. Its branches and leaves.
we follow the foliage. And not the location of the hole. Since it did not take root, its main part is not in the Land.
terumah etc.. Which includes also challah (Hilchot Bikkurim 5:5).
and even in the days of Ezra. In the Second Temple period.

as it says, "when you come into the land" - the coming of all of you. This verse is stated regarding the commandment of libations, and the Sages learned that the same law applies to terumot (see Yad Peshutah).
when they were in the first inheritance. The conquest of those who came up from Egypt.
in the third inheritance. At the end of the Second Temple exile.
any food of man. Which people are accustomed to eat, and see below, halachot 2-5.
that is guarded. That is not ownerless, and see below, halachot 9-12.
whose growth is from the earth. Excluding truffles and mushrooms, which do not draw nourishment from the soil like other plants (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 2:2).
the first of your grain, your wine, and your oil etc. you shall give him. This is the commandment of terumah, that a person give to the kohen the first gift of those crops.
grain. The five species of grain.
wine. Grape wine.
and oil. Olive oil.
and it has owners, as it says "your grain". The grain that belongs to you.
vetch. A kind of legume (called in our day bitter vetch) used mainly as animal fodder.
se'ah, hyssop, and koranit. Wild plants used, among other things, for seasoning and animal fodder.
and he designated them for people while they were attached. He changed their designation, before they were picked.
for a designation while attached is nothing. Rather the intention at the time of sowing.
grew by themselves in the courtyard. Se'ah hyssop or koranit that grew wild.
a courtyard that guards its produce. Whose produce is guarded.
for by default they are for people. By default they are intended for human use.
garden seeds that are not eaten. Seeds that are not eaten themselves, but are sown to grow edible vegetables.

caper. The caper bush has three edible parts: tamarot, which are the buds of the plant (Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 4:6; some explain they are the young branches), kafrisin, which are dry parts resembling wood and leaves (there; some explain they are the fruit buds), and avyonot, which are the final fruit.
because they are not fruit. Rather their seeds are considered the fruit of those species.
if he sowed them for seed. For eating the seeds.
but if he sowed them for greens. To eat the green parts of the plant.
coriander. Coriander.
that he sowed for seed. For using its seeds as food.
its greens. Its green leaves.

he sowed it for greens, he separates terumah and ma'aserot from the greens and from the seed. For in this plant the seed is the main part and therefore he always separates from it, but if he intended to use the leaves, they too are considered the fruit of the plant.
and likewise dill. A seasoning plant (called in our day shamir).
stalks. The stems.
cress. Cultivated cress, which can be eaten as is, or ground and used as seasoning or medicine.
and rocket. A plant identified today as a kind of mustard and known today as rocket leaves.
that he sowed for seed are tithed as both seed and greens. With cress and rocket it is customary to eat the greens as well, and therefore he separates from both.
how are they tithed for seed and for greens etc.. For picking for the sake of eating greens or seed do not happen at the same time.
grain and the like. For example legumes.

and so it appears to me that the same is true of terumah etc.. Although the term "grain" is mentioned only regarding tithe to exempt greens, in terumah too greens are exempt by Torah law, for things like grain, wine, and oil are not greens.
from greens outside the Land. From greens that grew outside the Land.
and even in the places in which we said they separate tithes. As above 1:1-6.

and likewise greens that come from outside the Land into the Land. Unlike crops whose obligation is essentially by Torah law, which, if brought to the Land of Israel, have an obligation of separation in certain circumstances (see above 1:22-23).
even though there is dirt on their roots. Although there is soil attached to the roots, this is not considered as if it is attached and continues to grow in the soil of the Land of Israel.

his intention is nullified in the view of everyone etc.. This is unusual behavior, since it is not the way of people to eat the leaves of grain and legumes but their seeds, and therefore his intention is not considered at all.
fenugreek. Fenugreek.
even though it is not human food once it hardens. When the seed grows and hardens, it is not fit for human consumption.

since most people eat them in their early stage, they are obligated in terumah and ma'aserot. Many people are accustomed to eat the seeds at the beginning of their growth, while soft, and therefore the species is obligated in terumot and ma'aserot, although afterward it is not fit for human food.
leket, forgotten sheaves, pe'ah etc.. All these are gifts to the poor, which the poor gather from the field, vineyard, and tree (Leviticus 19:9-10, Deuteronomy 24:19-21, Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 1:1-7).
even if he made a pile of them. Even if the poor person gathered so much that he made a heap.

and if he made a threshing floor of them in the field etc.. If he moved them to a place where grain is threshed and sorted, as the owner of a field does with his crop, he is obligated to separate, because onlookers assume that he made this threshing floor from the produce of his own field.

if he made the threshing floor in the city, they are exempt, for they have a reputation etc.. If he did these same actions in the city, onlookers know that he brought them little by little from various places and that they are from gifts to the poor (Rashi, Sotah 43b).

leket, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah of a gentile are obligated in terumah and ma'aserot. Since a gentile is not obligated to give leket, forgotten sheaves, and pe'ah, their law remains like that of any gentile's crop in the Land of Israel, which is obligated in terumah and ma'aserot (above 1:11-12).
unless he declared it ownerless. For all ownerless produce is exempt from terumah and ma'aserot, as below, halachah 11, and in this a gentile is equal to an Israelite.

grain and olives that had not reached a third. That did not reach a third of their growth. For reaching a third is their "time of the tithes," and only from then on are they obligated (see Hilchot Ma'aser 2:5, and see there the definition of "a third" with regard to olives).
anything that he sows and it sprouts. He sows the kernels in it, and they grow.
ownerless produce. Produce with no owner, or whose owners let anyone take it and are not particular about it (Derech Emunah, based on Hilchot Ma'aser 1:12).

and even if the gentile declared it ownerless. Although his fruits that grew in the Land of Israel are in principle obligated in terumah and ma'aserot (see above 1:11), if he declared them ownerless they are like all ownerless fruit.
but one who sows an ownerless field is obligated in terumah and ma'aserot. Since the grain is not ownerless but only the field.
standing grain. Grain that has not been harvested.

and he transgressed and separated terumah from it, it is terumah etc.. The basis of the difference between the two cases is that one cannot separate terumah and ma'aserot from standing grain, whereas from the ears one can (even though they have not reached completion of work). This difference affects the meaning of declaring ownerless with regard to terumah and ma'aserot: declaring standing grain ownerless has no meaning of exemption from the tithes, and therefore if he returned and acquired it and separated from it, the terumah takes effect. But if he declared ears ownerless, that is, after the grain was harvested, this has the meaning of exempting from the law of terumah and ma'aserot, and therefore even if he separates from the ears after he returns and acquires them, the terumah does not take effect.
but their presumption is from ownerless produce. For generally they grow wild.
bachi garlic and Rekpa onion. A type of very sharp garlic and onion, named for the place of their origin.
and Cilician split beans. The half-kernel of a large, square fava bean found in Cilicia.
and Egyptian lentils. Lentils with a pointed end (Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aserot 5:7).
nikuf olives. Olives that remain after the harvest, which are gathered by the poor and exempt from terumot and ma'aserot (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Pe'ah 8:3, Chalah 6:9).
with harvest olives. That were harvested by the owner of the olives and are obligated in terumah and ma'aserot.
olelot. A small cluster of grapes that must be left for the poor (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 4:17).
with vintage grapes. That were harvested by the owner of the vineyard.

if he has other fruit, he takes out for the obligated part proportionally. If he has other tevel fruit of the same kind, he can separate from it also for the tevel that became mixed, according to the quantity of tevel in the mixture.

and if he has only these etc.. If he has no other tevel fruit, he separates from the mixture itself, all of which is considered tevel to be forbidden (see Hilchot Bikkurim 7:11). However, he takes out the terumot in proportion to the quantity of all the fruit in the mixture, since they were stringent regarding terumot because of the death penalty at the hands of Heaven that attaches to them (Commentary on the Mishnah, Chalah 3:9), whereas the ma'aserot he separates only according to the measure of the tevel that is mixed in.
terumah is for the kohen, whether impure or pure. Terumah is given to a kohen even if it is not pure and he cannot eat it (and see below 3:1 that today every terumah is treated as impure).
my terumot. In the plural, and from here the Sages learned that impure terumah must also be given to the kohen.
and the impure, they will benefit from its burning. For the benefit from its burning belongs to the kohanim.
as we have explained in Berachot. Hilchot Berachot 11:2-3.
until it becomes impure with an impurity known to all. That it becomes impure in a clear way, and then its law is like that of any impure terumah.
until the eve of Passover if it is chametz, and it is burned. Because of the prohibition of chametz (see also Hilchot Bikkurim 5:7).

and one does not bring terumah from outside the Land. From places where the Sages obligated terumah (see above 1:1-6), so that the kohanim will not go out to outside the Land to those places to bring terumah from there to the Land (Jerusalem Talmud, Shevi'it 6:4).
because it is impure in the land of the nations. For the Sages decreed impurity on outside the Land (Hilchot Tumat Met, chapter 11).
and it is not burned. Like impure terumah (as above, halachah 14).

so that they will not say, "we saw terumah that had not become impure being burned". For the law of the impurity of the land of the nations is not known to all and they might think that the terumah was burned although it had not become impure at all.
it has no measure by Torah law. No specific measure was set for it.
even one grain of wheat exempts the heap. A single kernel of terumah suffices to exempt an entire pile.

and nowadays when it is destined to be burned because of impurity. For today there is no way to be purified from corpse impurity, and the kohanim and the terumah become impure, and the terumah is forbidden for eating and must be burned.
he may initially separate any amount. A very small quantity, by the law of the Torah.
a good eye. A term for generosity.
and the medium. Average.
and an evil eye. A term for stinginess.
any terumah that the kohanim are not particular about. The quality of the fruit is very low.
and the kelisin. The Rambam identified the kelisin as a kind of small figs (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 11:4), and some wrote that these are the fruit of the field jujube.
growths of terumah. One who sows terumah and it produced crops: their law is like chullin that require separation of terumot and ma'aserot, but they are forbidden to non-kohanim (below 11:21).

and mixtures of terumah. Terumah that became mixed with tevel, and one must separate to make the tevel part fit for eating. The entire mixture is permitted for eating to kohanim alone, and therefore he separates the small measure by the law of growths of terumah (Derech Emunah, Yad Peshutah).
and impure terumah where the impurity was by accident or inadvertently. Terumah separated from produce that became impure unintentionally.
and terumah of consecrated produce. Terumah from produce that was consecrated after it became obligated in terumot and ma'aserot.
and terumah from outside the Land. In places where the Sages ordained an obligation of separation (see above 1:6).
and the gimziyot. Fruit that grows on the trunk of barren trees, such as the sycamore and the carob (Tosefta Kifshutah, Pesachim p. 361).
and lupines. A kind of legume.
and red barley. Which is an inferior kind of barley.
and fruit of a pot that is not perforated. Which is obligated in terumah and ma'aserot only by rabbinic law (below 5:15-16).
the trustees. Those appointed to manage the property of minor orphans; they set right the tevel (untithed produce) of the orphans so they may eat it (Hilchot Nachalot 11:9).

this terumah may not be separated by measure... because no fixed amount was stated for it. The terumah should not be measured in these ways, because by Torah law it has no defined amount, and if he measures it, it will look as though that is the Torah's commandment (Kesef Mishneh). Some explained that the very act of measuring shows disrespect, so it is to be avoided when the Torah gives no explicit commandment for it (see Yad Peshutah).
but he may separate terumah from produce that has been measured, weighed or counted. He may separate terumah from measured produce, but he may not measure the terumah itself.

nor may he separate terumah using a basket or a kupah whose capacity is known, etc.. He should not place the terumah in a vessel whose size is known, since that is like measuring with it, but he may fill part of it.
nor may he separate terumah using half a se'ah, because half is a measure. Since it is customary to measure even by filling half the se'ah measure.
one who gives more terumah than required. That is, he gives more than the set amount.
has said nothing. The commandment is to separate terumah from the crop, and if he gives all of it as terumah, he has not separated anything from it.

one who intended to separate one tenth and ended up with one sixtieth, his terumah is terumah. Although he actually separated less than he planned, the separation is valid and the produce is rectified.
if he intended to separate one sixtieth, etc.. If he ended up with more than he thought to separate, this is contrary to his intention, so the separation is not valid and the produce is still tevel.
one who separates terumah, etc.. If he had no particular amount in mind to take and it turned out that he took more than the Sages set, the separation is nevertheless valid.

that excess is subject to tithes, etc.. Since it was separated after the terumah had already been separated, the excess does not count as terumah, and it has the status of the rest of the produce from which terumah gedolah was separated, which is subject to the other tithes (D.A.).
he separated terumah and ended up with one sixty-first. If he unintentionally took less than the Sages set.
it is terumah. The separation counts as terumah.
and he should separate terumah a second time to complete the amount he had in mind. And this addition too counts as terumah.

and this addition he may separate by measure, etc.. He may separate it even by measuring (which was forbidden above, halacha 5), because the main giving was done in the permitted manner (Yad Peshutah).
from the surrounding produce. From the pile in front of him, and not from produce in another place (below, halacha 17).
as the first. Like the law of the first terumah he separated.

one who separates part of the terumah, that part is not terumah, etc.. If at first he deliberately took out only part of what he planned to separate, the separation is not valid and it is not terumah, but remains tevel like the rest of the produce, as if he had divided the tevel pile into two.

and nevertheless, etc.. Although the part separated is considered tevel, they were strict about it, that he may not combine it with other tevel and separate from the other for both (as below, halacha 18); rather he must separate from within it.
if he separated part of the terumah, etc.. If he has two piles and from each he separated less than he planned, he may not separate from one of them on behalf of both.
one who says, etc.. When he performs the separation.

if he said, 'in its north' or 'in its south,' he has designated a place, and he must separate his terumah from it. If he explicitly specified the place of the terumah in the pile, the specified part is given the name of terumah and the separation is valid, and he must take out what he separated and give it to the kohen in accordance with the law of terumah.
and if he did not designate a place, etc.. If he did not specify a particular place in the pile, his words have no effect.
the terumah of this pile and of that pile, in this one. That he separates the terumah of both piles from one of them (and see Radbaz and Kesef Mishneh, who had a different reading here).

the place where the first one's terumah was fixed, there the second one's terumah is fixed. If he specified the place of the terumah of one pile (for example, in its north), the place of the second pile's terumah is next to it.
terumat ma'aser. The separation of a tenth from the first tithe, which is given to the kohanim as terumah.

and even at the present time. When the terumah is destined to be burned, one cannot separate any amount at all as is done for terumah gedolah (above, halacha 1), because the amount of terumat ma'aser is stated explicitly in the Torah, and if he separates less than that, the tithe will not become permitted for eating.
something that is normally measured. By volume.
and something that can be counted. By its individual units.
one who counts is praiseworthy. More than one who separates by estimate and not exactly.

it is a commandment that a Levite separate terumat ma'aser, etc.. The obligation to separate terumat ma'aser from the first tithe falls primarily on the Levite, since the command to separate it was addressed to the Levites.
and an Israelite may separate it, etc.. The owner of the crop may separate it himself from the tithe and give it to the kohen, and afterward give the rest of the tithe to the Levite.
who separated the first tithe while it was still in ears. Before the kernels were separated from the harvested grain, when it was not yet obligated in terumah.
but if he threshed. After threshing and smoothing the pile, the grain became obligated in terumah (Hilchot Ma'aser 3:13).
a Levite who took the tithe in ears. He needs to separate only terumat ma'aser and is exempt from terumah gedolah, as above.

rather, we penalize him by making him thresh and winnow, etc.. To process the grain himself and to give the kohen terumat ma'aser from the produce, because he took the tithe at a time that removed from it the obligation of terumah gedolah.
a tithe from the tithe. Terumat ma'aser (following the wording of the verse, Numbers 18:28).

and he need not give him the tithe of the straw or the chaff. Although the tithe he received from the ears included the straw in which the kernels were, nevertheless once he has separated the kernels from it, the straw is his.
and if he separated terumat ma'aser while in ears. And again acted improperly.

he must pound and give the kohen the grain and the straw. The Sages penalized him: he must see to separating the kernels from the ears, and give terumat ma'aser both from the grain and from the waste.
and why did they penalize him to pound?. Why can he not give terumat ma'aser from the ears?
because he took the tithe in ears and removed terumah gedolah from it. And thereby caused the kohanim a certain loss.
my father told me thus: 'I have a tithe for you in my hand'. My father told me before his death to give you this tithe.
we do not suspect about the terumat ma'aser in it. There is no need to separate terumat ma'aser from that tithe, as we assume that the father separated it himself.

'I have a kor of tithe for you in my hand,' we suspect about its terumat ma'aser. For if the father specified the quantity of the tithe, it is understood that he did so in order that the Levite would know how much terumat ma'aser must be separated from it.
terumat ma'aser, etc.. And the same law applies to terumah gedolah (D.A.).
one-eighth of an eighth. One sixty-fourth of a log (about 5 milliliters).
less than this, he does not trouble himself to take it, etc.. In a smaller amount, there is no need to bother bringing it to the kohen, because it is of no importance.
but with wine and oil, even any amount, etc.. Because there is benefit in every drop of them, in drinking (Yad Peshutah).
if it was impure. So that it cannot be drunk and its law is to be burned.

or if it was demai. Produce about which there is doubt whether it is tevel or tithed; the Sages ordained that he separate tithes from it (Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1). In this case, even with pure wine and oil the Sages did not trouble him.
but only from the surrounding produce. Produce lying together, as will be explained in the next halacha.
and if he separated not from the surrounding produce, his terumah is terumah. If he transgressed and separated, the terumah takes effect.

provided that what was separated is guarded. Separation not from the surrounding produce is effective only if he separates something that is kept, and not something that will be lost (following the Radbaz; and the Riko explained that the law of 'guarded' applies also to separation from the surrounding produce).
a load. That which is carried.
storehouses. Storage vessels.
if they were in one enclosure. Placed together.

barrels of wine before he sealed their openings, etc.. That he may separate from one on behalf of all only while they are open, for once sealed each barrel stands on its own, even if the barrels are adjacent.
bundles of vegetables. Bunches of vegetables (Tosefta Ki-Fshutah, Terumot p. 326).
he separates from one on behalf of all. Because the garden regards them as one unit.
if he brought a different kind among them. If there was also another type of vegetable in the garden, between the piles of the same kind.
he separates from each one individually. From each pile separately, since the garden no longer joins them.
in a kupah. A kind of basket.
he may not separate from the upper on behalf of the lower. Although the kupah is a single place, the separation by a different kind makes them count as two places.
and if he gathered five heaps on the threshing floor. If he placed five piles together around the place where the grain is threshed.

as long as the main threshing floor remains. That there is still grain in the middle that has not been cleared away, so that it is evident that all the piles are placed around it for the same purpose.
as it is said, 'from all your tithes,' etc.. Regarding terumat ma'aser, and from this they learned that one may separate from wherever the produce is, even if it is not adjacent.

and he left it to keep separating from it as he goes along, while it is still in its tevel state. He left it as tevel and did not separate terumat ma'aser from it, in order to use part of it each time as terumat ma'aser for other tithes in his possession, and finally to give all of it to the kohen.

'For the tithe of the children of Israel, which they set apart as a gift to the Lord'. The tithe received by the Levites is also called terumah, and from here the Sages learned that the entire tithe can be made terumat ma'aser.
as it is said, 'its holy part from it'. The full verse: 'Out of all your gifts you shall set apart every gift due to the Lord, from all the best of it, its holy part from it.'

when its holy parts are within it, etc.. From the words 'its holy part from it' they learned that only if the holy part, namely the terumat ma'aser, is still within the tithe can the whole tithe be made terumah for others. But if it was separated from the tithe, he cannot use the rest as terumat ma'aser for others.
and likewise one who sets aside produce to keep separating terumah gedolah on their behalf. He designated certain produce to take the terumah from it for other produce that is tevel.
they must be subject to terumah, etc.. That they themselves must be obligated in the separation of terumah gedolah, and similarly with the law of the tithe.
he first separates the first fruits from everything. The fruit that grew first (see Hilchot Bikkurim 2:19).

second tithe or poor man's tithe. Depending on the year: in the first, second, fourth and fifth years of the Sabbatical cycle he separates second tithe; and in the third and sixth years he separates the poor man's tithe.
and one is not flogged for this prohibition. Because it is like a prohibition that is linked to a positive commandment (see Radbaz).

one who wishes to separate terumah gedolah and terumat ma'aser together. To take out together all the gifts for the kohen, which are forbidden to non-kohanim to eat, and then the rest of the produce is permitted for eating immediately.
he separates one thirty-third and a third. Which is three percent of the produce.

the one percent that is here is beside this which I have separated, and it is chullin (ordinary produce). He designates the place of one percent of the three relative to the other two, and leaves it for now as chullin, in order to define it afterward as terumat ma'aser.

and what remains of this which I have separated is terumah on everything. The other two percent he designates as terumah gedolah on all the produce, as the measure of a medium eye, which is one fiftieth.

and the tithe that should be for these hundred of chullin is beside this which I have separated. Afterward he designates as first tithe a tenth of the produce, which is the one percent out of the three percent he specified at the beginning, and nine percent of the produce adjacent to it.
and this remainder, etc.. And he adds and designates as terumat ma'aser that same percent that was set aside earlier.
'So you also shall set apart,' to include the agent. From the extra word 'also' the Sages learned that others too can separate as agents of the owner of the produce.

and one does not appoint a gentile as an agent. Because a gentile is not considered the agent of an Israelite to be like him (see Hilchot Ishut 3:17, Hilchot Zechiyah UMatanah 4:6, Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 2:1).

'you' - as you are members of the covenant. From the word 'you' they learned that the possibility of appointing an agent is limited to one who is like you, a member of the covenant, namely an Israelite who made a covenant with the Holy One, blessed be He.
a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor. Who lack understanding.
and a gentile who separated terumah of an Israelite's produce, even with his permission. Since a gentile does not become an agent of an Israelite (above, halacha 1).
and one who separates terumah from what is not his. He separates from his fellow's produce to make it permitted, as below, halacha 3.
and the benefit. The right to decide to whom the terumah is given.
one who separates without permission. He separated from his fellow's produce in order to make it permitted.
and gathered produce without permission in order to take it. For himself (Riko and other commentators).
and separated terumah. From that same produce, in order to rectify it.
go to the nicer ones. Go and separate from better produce.
for he is not particular. His words were said in earnest, and it is evident that he agreed to the separation of the terumah.
for he said it to him only as a protest. His words were a protest against his separating the finest produce, and he did not agree to the separation.
and if the householder came and gathered and added, etc.. He added produce to what the first had separated as terumah, so it is evident from his actions that he agreed to the first one's terumah.
because he does not hear the blessing. And by strict law the one who recites a blessing must hear it (see Hilchot Berachot 1:7), therefore he should not separate ab initio.
a mute and a naked person, because they cannot bless. A mute cannot bless, and a naked person is forbidden to bless until he covers his nakedness (ibid. 1:9).

a minor who has reached the age for vows. A boy from the age of thirteen years and a day, and a girl from twelve years and a day. From this age they are obligated to fulfill their vows (see Hilchot Nedarim 11:1-4).

even though he has not grown two hairs and has not become an adult. Which are the signs of adulthood of a male and a female (see Hilchot Ishut chapter 2); in other matters their acts have no legal validity without these signs.
since their vows and their consecrations are valid. And terumah is similar to a vow and a consecration (see below, halacha 17, and below 7:1).
as we explained regarding vows. Hilchot Nedarim 11:1-4.
and he came and found his pile separated as terumah. It is evident that terumah was separated from it.

for we do not say, in matters of prohibition, that an agent is presumed to have carried out his mission, to be lenient. In matters of prohibition we rely on the assumption that an agent did what he was sent to do when this leads to stringency (see Hilchot Ishut 9:6), but we do not rely on this assumption to be lenient.
and he suspects that perhaps someone separated without permission. We must be concerned that another person separated without permission, and his separation has no validity.
one with a grudging eye, etc.. The three measures that the Sages set for terumah (above 3:2).
one of generous spirit. One who lacks nothing, who would presumably give with a generous eye.
he intended the medium measure. He intended to separate one fiftieth.
his terumah is terumah. Since he intended to separate properly.

but if he intended to add to the medium... his terumah is not terumah. If from the outset he intended to separate more than the medium amount, the terumah does not take effect, since he separated deliberately in an improper manner.
as it is said, 'your tithes'. In the plural, to include partners.

if they were protesting against each other, etc.. If each one protested to the other not to separate, the one who went first, his terumah is terumah, since he may separate even without permission, as above. However, the protest has the effect that the second cannot add terumah to the first one's terumah, even if the first separated less than the amount (following the Riko; and see Kesef Mishneh and Radbaz, who explained differently).
and if they did not protest and the first separated the proper amount. That the Sages set as the medium measure, namely one fiftieth (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 3:3).

the second's terumah is not terumah. That even if they did not protest against each other, if the first separated the proper amount, the second's terumah is not terumah. For once it has been separated in the proper amount, it is not possible to add to the terumah (see above 3:6).

and if the first did not separate the proper amount, the terumah of both is terumah. For when neither protested, both can separate, and the second's addition counts as terumah until the terumah amount is filled (see there).
and he canceled their agency. He regretted appointing them as his agents.

if the agent did not change, his terumah is terumah. Since the rule is that agency cannot be canceled by words alone (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 3:4; and see the Riko and Radbaz, that this rule applies to terumah but not to all laws).

and if he changed... since he canceled his agency beforehand, it is not terumah. Although a cancellation by itself and such a change by itself are not enough to invalidate the separation, their combination together is effective (see the Riko and Radbaz).
a sharecropper. A worker who works the field in return for a certain percentage of the crop.
and the householder came and objected. He opposed the separation.

and if he objected after he had separated, his terumah is terumah. Because he separated with permission, for the householder presumably agrees that he separate, as long as he has not revealed that he does not agree to this.

and the trustees. Guardians appointed to manage the property of orphans. [Note: the vocalization of the word follows the Greek original. In the Commentary on the Mishnah in Maimonides' own hand, several vocalizations of this word appear: sometimes the first pe is vocalized with a kubutz, sometimes with a patach (and in some places the pe has no vowel).]
may separate terumah from orphans' property. Without their knowledge, so that the orphans will have something to eat (see Hilchot Nachalot 11:9).
a thief, a robber and a forcible taker. Who took produce that is not theirs and separated terumah from it.
and a forcible taker. Who compels the owners to give him what is theirs.
their terumah is terumah. Because they acquired the item through the owners' despair of recovering it.
and if the owners were pursuing them, etc.. Trying to get back what is theirs, which shows that they had not despaired.
they separate terumah only on what they eat. When they eat from the householder's produce, they do not separate on all the produce, but only on what they take to eat.
for a person cannot separate terumah from something that is not his. And they are not the owners of all the property, nor even partners, but have permission to eat only.
a son when his father eats. When he gives his father to eat from the father's property (Yad Peshutah).
and a woman with her dough. When she prepares bread also for her husband, and separates challah from it.
those who tread in the winepress. Workers who tread the grapes in the winepress in the process of producing wine.

for if they wished to make the wine impure, they could make it impure immediately, etc.. Since the grapes were pressed and became wine, they are susceptible to impurity. And because he handed responsibility for the winepress to the workers, and relied on them not to make the wine impure, they are considered his agents also for the separation of terumah.

'Gather in my threshing floor'. He told him to bring the produce from the threshing floor into his possession, and since 'a threshing floor is not brought in unless terumah has been separated' (Tosefta, Terumot 1:7), this command includes the instruction to separate terumah.
and he separated terumah and afterward gathered it, his terumah is terumah. But if he separated and did not gather it in, his terumah is not terumah (Tosefta Ki-Fshutah p. 299).
by Torah law. By strict law.

a decree because of the wealthy, etc.. Rich people who want to evade separating terumah and tithes, who might sell their grain to a gentile before smoothing so that the gentile will smooth it and they will be exempt from tithes (since a gentile's smoothing exempts, as above 1:11). Therefore the Sages ordained that in such a case the grain is obligated in terumah and tithes (above 1:13). And to distance people further from using gentiles' grain, they decreed that if he separated from it, the terumah takes effect (Yad Peshutah).
we examine the gentile. For whose sake he separated the terumah.
'I separated it with the intention of an Israelite'. In the way Israelites separate it, whose intention is to give to the kohanim.
it requires being hidden away, lest in his heart he dedicated it to Heaven. Perhaps he intended to dedicate it to the Temple, and it is forbidden to use this money (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 8:8).
outside the Land of Israel. In places where terumah and tithes are obligated rabbinically.
one who intends to say. When he separates and designates by name.
until his mouth and his heart are equal. That the words he intended in his heart to say come out of his mouth, and not something else.
by thought alone it becomes terumah. Without speech, and also without actually separating from the rest of the produce (Riko).
and he regretted it. He changed his mind and regretted the separation.

he may ask a Sage about it, who releases it for him, as other vows are released. He can ask a Sage to annul the separation, for the law of terumah is like that of vows, which a Sage can release (see Hilchot Shevu'ot chapter 6, Hilchot Nedarim 4:5, 4:7).
and it returns to being chullin as it was. The terumah returns to being part of the rest of the produce as it was, with no holiness in it.
on condition that it come up whole. He separated on the condition that the terumah take effect only if the barrel containing the terumah comes up from the cistern intact.
whole from breaking and from spilling. The condition refers only to the possibility that the barrel will break near the cistern or that the wine will spill back into the cistern.
but not from impurity. For if what was separated became impure, the condition does not cancel the separation.

and if it broke, it does not cause diluted terumah (it does not render other produce forbidden). Since the condition was effective in canceling the separation, if some of the wine from the barrel spilled into the cistern, the wine in the cistern does not have the law of a mixture of terumah and chullin, and it is permitted to non-kohanim.

it causes such status, since its condition was already fulfilled. For if afterward some of the wine that was separated spilled into the cistern, the separation is not canceled. Once the terumah was placed at a reasonable distance from the cistern, it is considered to have come up whole, and the condition was fulfilled.

in what case does this apply? To terumah gedolah. Which must be separated from the surrounding produce, so the terumah must be separated from the wine in the cistern. Therefore the condition includes the possibility that the barrel will break even after it has come up from the cistern until it is set down at a distant place.
but with terumat ma'aser, which may be separated not from the surrounding produce. As above 3:20.

once it came up, his condition was fulfilled, etc.. For he stipulated only about mishaps that might occur during the separation itself; had he been concerned also about damage occurring after it came up from the cistern, he could have separated from the outset not from the surrounding produce and avoided such damage (following Yad Peshutah).
and needless to say if it became impure. That the separation is not canceled, since even with terumah gedolah the separation is valid in this case.
what is above is terumah. He specified that the place of the terumah would be in the upper part of the crop.
the pile. The heap itself.
that which is in the broken pieces. Produce that scattered from the heap and is collected separately.
that which is at the sides. A single kernel separated from the heap.
and what is within the straw. Kernels mixed in the pile of straw.
one who separates the winevat, etc.. He separates the wine while it is in the vat where grapes are trodden, where the skins and seeds remain from which wine can still be extracted.

one who separates the wine cistern... on what is in the grape-skins. After treading, the wine flows with the grape refuse into the cistern, and the refuse settles at its bottom. After the wine is removed from the cistern, wine can be extracted from it.

for it is a condition of the court that the terumah is on everything. The Sages established that this is the manner of separation, so every unspecified separation is made on the basis of this condition.
a basket. A basket.
terumah is separated only from the best. From the choicest part of the crop.
its fat. The choicest part.
and if there is no kohen there. But rather in a distant place, and the terumah may spoil before it reaches him.
he separates from that which keeps. From what is preserved for a long time until the terumah reaches the kohen.
he separates figs on behalf of dried figs. For fresh figs are better than dried figs ('geroggerot').
and in a place where there is no kohen he separates dried figs on behalf of figs. Because dried figs keep.
and if he is accustomed to make his figs into dried figs. If it is his practice to dry his figs.

he separates from figs on behalf of dried figs, even in a place where there is no kohen. In case a kohen happens by and he brings him the better figs. And there is no concern that the terumah will spoil before reaching a kohen, since after he separates from the fresh figs he will make them into dried figs.

but in a place where there is a kohen, one does not separate from dried figs on behalf of figs, etc.. For fresh figs are better, and he can separate from the choice produce and give it to the kohen immediately.
and one separates a whole onion... in any place. Whether or not there is a kohen there, since a whole onion is considered better than half of a large onion, and it also keeps.
one does not separate from one kind on behalf of what is not its kind. From one type of crop on behalf of another type.

like the grain from the threshing floor. One must separate the grain on behalf of what is on the threshing floor, and the continuation of the verse, 'and as the fullness from the winepress,' means wine on behalf of what is in the winepress. From here we learn that from each kind one separates for itself.
kishut (a type of cucumber-like gourd). A kind of gourd resembling a cucumber.
all kinds of wheat. All types of wheat.
and a cake of dried figs. A lump of dried figs.

and anything that is kilayim with another, one may not separate from one on behalf of the other. Any two kinds that are forbidden to sow together are considered two kinds also for terumah (the definitions of the kinds for this purpose are detailed in Hilchot Kilayim 3:1-6).
and anything that is not kilayim with another. Whatever is considered one kind for kilayim and may be sown together.
he separates from the better on behalf of the worse. From the better kind on behalf of that which is inferior to it (as above, halacha 1).

except from tares on behalf of wheat, because tares are not human food. Tares are an inferior kind of wheat. And although with regard to the prohibition of kilayim they are one kind (Hilchot Kilayim 3:3), separation from them on behalf of wheat is not valid, because they are not human food and are exempt from terumah and tithes (above 2:1), and one does not separate from the exempt on behalf of the obligated.
once he has sifted. Once he separates the kernels from the refuse using a coarse sieve (a kevarah).
he sifted some. He sifted a little, and then it counts as the completion of the work of everything, because not everyone is particular about sifting the grain before bringing it home (Yad Peshutah).
he separates from the sifted on behalf of the unsifted. For it is from the better.
to make them melilot. To eat the soft kernels from the ears, in which case their work is considered complete even while they are still ears.
the winepress. The place where grapes are trodden.
once they have walked on it. Those who tread on the grapes.
warp and woof. Lengthwise and crosswise.
from when may olives be separated?. Those meant for producing oil.
once they are piled up. Olives are stored before pressing in a vessel called a ma'aten, so that they soften.
and it is a halacha to Moses from Sinai. A legal tradition.

that a round cake of dried figs a part of which became impure. A round cake of dried figs is made of many dried figs pressed together, and if one spot in it becomes impure, all of it is not impure, because they are regarded as separate pieces.
one may separate ab initio from the pure part of it on behalf of the impure part. Because for this purpose it is like a single unit.
even a pile of wheat. Although nothing joins them together, its law is like that of a cake of dried figs, that they are regarded as a single whole.
as it is said. Regarding terumat ma'aser.
take from the consecrated part of it. The Sages explained that the consecrated is the pure, and one may separate from it even if the rest is impure.
if deliberately, he has not rectified the remainder, etc.. If he separated from the impure deliberately, the Sages penalized him: the rest is still considered tevel and must be separated from again.
and this which he separated as terumah. What he separated from the impure has the status of terumah, and does not return to being chullin.
in what case? Where he did not know about the impurity. The 'inadvertent' here means that he did not know that he was separating from the impure on behalf of the pure.

but if he knew and erred, thinking it permitted to separate... it is as if deliberate. Although in other commandments such ignorance counts as inadvertence (see for example Hilchot Shegagot 7:2-4), here they penalized him because he is an inadvertent offender close to a deliberate one, who should have known the law (Yad Peshutah).
and likewise with terumat ma'aser. For regarding separation from the impure on behalf of the pure, its law is like terumah gedolah.
one may not separate from attached produce. Crop that has not been harvested.

'This produce shall be terumah on that attached produce,' even if he said 'when they are detached,' etc.. Even in this case it is not terumah, because when he said 'the attached' it implies that he wants the terumah to take effect on the produce while still attached, even though he said 'when they are detached' (following Yad Peshutah; Kesef Mishneh corrected and read 'even when they are detached,' meaning that the terumah does not take effect even if the produce is detached afterward, since he separated the terumah on attached produce).

or if he had two beds and said, 'the produce of this bed, when detached, shall be terumah on the produce of this bed, attached'. Where all the produce is still attached, but he says that when the produce of one bed is detached he will separate from it on behalf of the attached; even so the terumah does not take effect, for it is like separating from the detached on behalf of the attached.

or if he said, 'the produce of this bed, detached, shall be terumah on the produce of this bed, detached,' etc.. And the produce is still attached, because the meaning of the words is that the terumah should take effect now, and one cannot separate from attached produce on behalf of attached produce.
when they are detached. For it is clear from his words that he wants the terumah to take effect only after the produce is detached.
since it is in his power to detach them... his words stand. Since detaching is an act that depends on him and he can do it right now himself, its lack is not significant.
provided that both have reached a third at the time he spoke. For that is the beginning of their obligation to tithes (as above 1:12 and Hilchot Ma'aser 2:3).

one does not separate from the moist on behalf of the dry, nor from the dry on behalf of the moist. One authority wrote that the reason is that moist and dry are like two kinds (Shakh, Yoreh De'ah 331, subsection 83), and see the Arukh HaShulchan (69:13), who wrote that one who separates from the dry on the moist is like one who separates from the inferior on the better, and the question remains why it is also forbidden to separate from the moist on the dry.
unless it is its practice to keep for two days. And both are moist.

as it is said, 'year by year'. The full verse: 'You shall surely tithe all the yield of your seed that comes forth from the field year by year.' From this the Sages learned that the crop of each year stands on its own regarding terumot and tithes.
before the sun came. Before sunset.

because the first of Tishrei is the new year for tithes of grain, etc.. And since for vegetables the time of picking defines the tithe year, vegetables picked before and after Rosh Hashanah are considered vegetables of different tithe years.

and likewise if he picked an etrog, etc.. The tithe year of tree fruit begins on the 15th of Shevat, so if he picked two etrogim, one before the 15th of Shevat and one on the 15th of Shevat, they belong to different tithe years (the tithe year of an etrog is determined by the date of its picking, unlike most fruits, whose tithe year is determined by the date when the fruit formed - before the 15th of Shevat or after; see there, halacha 5).
such as leket, shichechah and pe'ah. Above 2:9.

one who separates terumah from first tithe whose terumah has not been taken, etc.. Tithe that was separated after terumah gedolah and from which terumat ma'aser has not yet been separated. Although it is still obligated in separation, since it is not subject to terumah gedolah one cannot separate from it on behalf of other produce, for he would be separating from the exempt on behalf of the obligated.

or from second tithe or consecrated produce that have not been redeemed, etc.. For in order to eat second tithe produce it must be redeemed with money (see Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 4:1), and likewise in order to deconsecrate consecrated produce it must be redeemed (see Hilchot Erchin VeCharamim 6:4). And although they are still obligated in redemption, one cannot separate terumah gedolah from them, because they are not obligated in it and it counts as separating from the exempt on behalf of the obligated (and after they have been redeemed, certainly one cannot separate from them, Kesef Mishneh).

one does not separate from something obligated in terumah by Torah law, etc.. Since their obligations are not equal, it is like separating from the obligated on behalf of the exempt and from the exempt on behalf of the obligated (above, halacha 12).
and if he separated, his terumah is terumah, and he must separate again. See details below, halacha 16.
a perforated flowerpot. One that has a hole in its bottom.
it is like the ground. What is sown in it is as if it grew in the ground itself, and is obligated in terumah and tithes by Torah law.
the size of a small root. The thickness of a thin root that can connect to the ground through the hole, and because of this the plant is considered attached to the ground.

if he sowed grain in a pot that is not perforated and it reached a third. It grew to a third, which is the season of tithes for grain at which it becomes obligated in terumot and tithes (Hilchot Ma'aser 2:5).
and the grain was completed while it was perforated. The grain's growth was completed in a perforated pot.
it is regarded as growing in a non-perforated one. Because it reached the season of tithes when it was not perforated.
his terumah is terumah. Since both are obligated by Torah law, it is like separating from the obligated on behalf of the obligated.

if he separated from the non-perforated on behalf of the perforated, his terumah is terumah and he must separate again. What he separated counts as terumah and must be given to the kohen. However, since a non-perforated pot is not obligated in terumah by Torah law, this is like separating from the exempt on behalf of the obligated, and what was picked from the perforated pot is not released from its obligation and he must separate again for it.

from the perforated on behalf of the non-perforated, it is terumah. The produce in the non-perforated pot is permitted for eating, since the separation was made on it from produce whose obligation is not less than their own obligation.

and it may not be eaten until he separates terumah and tithes for it from another place. Since the non-perforated pot is exempt by Torah law from terumah, what he separated on its behalf from the perforated one is not terumah by strict law, but remains tevel and terumah and tithes must be separated on it to permit it for eating. And he must separate the terumot and tithes from other tevel produce and not from the terumah itself. The reason is that it has the name terumah, and if one separated from it itself, people would come to treat it lightly (Tosafot, Yevamot 89b).
demai. Produce about which there is doubt whether it has been tithed.

one who separates from demai on behalf of demai, and from demai on behalf of certain produce, etc.. When both are demai, perhaps only one is obligated, or perhaps both are obligated, or both exempt. And when he separates from demai on behalf of certain produce, perhaps he is separating from the obligated on behalf of the obligated, and perhaps from the exempt on behalf of the obligated. Therefore, when he separates from the demai he must separate again from what was separated on it, lest he separated from the exempt on behalf of the obligated. However, the terumah itself is permitted to the kohen even though he may have separated from the obligated on behalf of the exempt, for they were not strict to treat it as full tevel, since it was taken from demai, whose obligation is not certain (Rosh's commentary on Terumot 5:11).
if he separated from certain produce on behalf of demai, his terumah is terumah. And the demai is permitted.

and it may not be eaten until he separates terumah and tithes for it. Perhaps the demai is exempt, and he separated from the obligated on behalf of the exempt, and what he separated is not terumah and remains tevel.
ears on behalf of wheat. From ears of wheat on behalf of kernels of wheat whose work has been completed.

it is not terumah, a decree lest he trouble the kohen to pound and thresh. By strict law, one who separates from something whose work is not completed on behalf of something whose work is completed, after the fact his terumah takes effect (above 3:4), but the Sages decreed that he must separate again properly, so as not to trouble the kohen to complete the work on the terumah.

but one may separate oil on behalf of pickled olives, and wine on behalf of grapes to be made into raisins. Olives pickled for eating, and grapes that are dried to make raisins (and they are considered the same kind as the oil and the wine, although their uses differ).
to what is this similar? To one who separates from two kinds, etc.. As explained above, halacha 3.

one separates from oil olives on behalf of pickling olives. Oil olives are those meant for pressing out their oil, and they are rich in oil and more important than those fit only for pickling because of their little oil (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 2:6). The reason for this law, and for the following laws, is so that one separates from the better on behalf of the inferior and not the reverse.
the clear. Filtered wine.

from figs on behalf of dried figs by count, from dried figs on behalf of figs by measure... so that he always separates with a generous eye. Fresh figs are larger than dried figs, so when he separates from the fresh on behalf of the dried, he should separate according to the number of dried figs he wants to permit and not by volume, so that he separates a greater number of figs; whereas when he separates from the dried on behalf of the fresh, he should separate according to the volume of the fresh figs, so that he separates a greater number of dried figs, since their volume is smaller.

but not from bread on behalf of wheat, only by calculation. He must calculate the amount of wheat in the bread and separate in proportion to it, because bread is puffed with air and also contains other ingredients besides wheat.

and in all of these, if he separated, his terumah is terumah. After the fact, like one who separates from the inferior on behalf of the better; and likewise if he separated in a way that reduces the required amount, the separation is valid, since by strict law it suffices to separate any amount of terumah.
olives that are pounded. To produce oil from them.
grapes that are trodden. To produce wine from them.
on something whose work is not completed. Since the olives and grapes are still in the middle of the production process.
the first causes diluted terumah, etc.. The first, whose basis is from the law, if it became mixed with chullin, renders them forbidden for eating by an Israelite.
and one who eats it is liable for it like other full terumot. If deliberately, he is liable to death at the hand of Heaven, and if inadvertently, he pays the principal and adds a fifth (below 6:6).
but not the second. Because its basis is rabbinic.
and changed his mind. He changed his mind, and it turns out retroactively that when he separated, their work was not completed.
he need not separate again. Because the completion of the work is determined by his thought at the time of separation.

one does not separate vinegar on behalf of wine... for wine and vinegar are of one kind. But wine is considered better than vinegar, and therefore ab initio he should not separate from vinegar on behalf of wine, but he may separate from wine on behalf of vinegar.
and the vinegar that he separated turns out to be wine. After the separation it became clear that what he separated had not turned sour.
it is not terumah. Because he erred, for he did not intend to separate wine but vinegar, so the separation is void from the outset.

one who separates a barrel of wine on behalf of the wine and it turns out to be vinegar... it is not terumah. Because his intention was to separate from wine, and it became clear that at the time of separation it was already vinegar, and this is terumah given in error.
and likewise one who separates kishut and it turns out to be bitter. He separated a gourd on behalf of other gourds and it became clear afterward that it is bitter.
putrid. Spoiled.

or if they were found pecked at... and it was found uncovered, so that it is forbidden to drink. If the produce was pecked at or the wine was left uncovered, they are forbidden for eating and drinking out of concern that a snake ate or drank from them and left venom in them (Hilchot Rotzeach 11:7-8, 12:2).

terumah, and he must separate again. For all of these are considered a doubtful food (Riko, following the Jerusalem Talmud), and therefore it is uncertain whether the first terumah took effect or not.

and neither of them by itself causes diluted terumah, etc.. Since each one is of doubtful terumah status, if it became mixed into chullin, a hundred times as much is not required to nullify it (unless they fell in together, in which case one of them is certainly terumah), and likewise regarding liability for the fifth.
to another place. To other chullin.

they cause dilution like the smaller of the two. Although perhaps the larger is the terumah. By Torah law terumah is nullified by a majority and the Sages required a hundredfold, and in this case they were not strict, so it suffices that there be a hundred times the smaller and a majority against the larger (Radbaz).
one who tests the barrel. To make sure it has not turned sour, so that he can make it terumah on behalf of other wine.
and after some time he tested it and found it vinegar. And it is not known whether it was vinegar when he separated, for if it was vinegar it is not terumah (as above, halacha 22).

from the time he first tested it, for three days it is certainly wine. The souring process takes at least three days, and since when he tested it the previous time it was wine, certainly it was not vinegar during the three days after, and the separation of those days is valid.
in three periods. Three times a year, at which there are sharp changes in the weather that may affect the wine.
he must test the wine. Before he separates on it.
in the east wind at the end of the festival. When an east wind blows at the end of the festival of Sukkot.
and at the emergence of the semadar. When the blossoms fall and small grapes like clusters are visible.
and at the time when liquid enters the unripe grapes. When the unripe grapes fill with fluid.
and wine from its press. Must, squeezed grape juice.
one may separate on it on the presumption that it is wine for forty days. Even if one of the periods arrived within those days.

one who sets aside produce to separate on their behalf until they become terumah. And the produce he set aside is not before him and he does not know whether it still exists so that it can be made terumah.
