although one does not separate ab initio except from the surrounding produce. And after the fact the terumah is valid (above 3:17).
he found that they were lost. If after the separation it turned out that they were lost, and it is not known whether they existed when he separated.
who rebelled. Who refuses to live with him as husband and wife (see Hilchot Ishut 14:18).
these may eat. Since they have not yet left the kohen's possession.

terumah by Torah law may be eaten only by a kohen of established lineage. A kohen for whom there are witnesses as to who his fathers and his fathers' fathers were, kohanim, back to the kohanim who served in the Temple (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah chapter 20).
kohanim by presumption. A person presumed to be a kohen, but whose priestly lineage is not based on testimony (see there, halacha 1, that all kohanim in our time are kohanim by presumption).
with terumah of rabbinic origin. Whose obligation is rabbinic and not from the Torah; see above chapter 1.
and all amei ha'aretz (people unobservant of purity laws) are presumed impure. And they would unwittingly make the terumah impure.

therefore he may give impure terumah to any kohen he wishes. Even to a kohen who is an am ha'aretz, since it is known that the terumah is impure there is no concern that he will eat it (Mercheret HaMishneh and Arukh HaShulchan).
an Israelite woman. Whose father is not a kohen.
even a minor. Whose father marries her off (Hilchot Ishut 3:11).
a girl of three years and a day may eat. But before that she may not eat (see Riko).
and the breast and thigh. Gifts given to the kohen from certain offerings (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 9:11, 10:4).

and by Torah law she may eat once she is betrothed, etc.. Betrothal is the acquisition of kiddushin, whereas the chuppah is the stage of marriage in which the couple begin to live together (Hilchot Ishut 1:2, 10:1). By strict law she may eat terumah from the time of betrothal, and the Sages decreed that she may not eat until the chuppah.
a deaf woman... a deaf man. Who neither hear nor speak (Hilchot Ishut 2:26).
a deaf woman or an imbecile woman who married a kohen may not eat terumah. Because they cannot be acquired in kiddushin, as they lack understanding (see there 4:9).
even if her father married her off. The father of the deaf woman, and the kiddushin is valid by Torah law since it depends on her father's consent.
a decree lest a deaf kohen marry a deaf woman and feed her. And kiddushin of a deaf man is not valid by Torah law (there).
a non-kohen. One who is not a kohen.
as it is said, 'No lay person shall eat of the holy thing'. And terumah is called 'holy,' below 7:1.
his hired worker. A person hired to do work for the householder.
and a Hebrew slave is like a hired worker and a resident. Like the law of a hired worker and a resident (following the wording of the verse, Leviticus 25:40), and he is forbidden to eat terumah.
and a kohen's daughter married to a non-kohen. The daughter of a kohen who married a man who is not a kohen.
a non-kohen who ate terumah, etc.. See at length below, chapter 10.

'and die for it if they profane it'. In the verse after it, it says that a non-kohen may not eat holy things, and the Sages learned that regarding him too the punishment of death is stated (Sefer HaMitzvot, negative commandment 133).

that he is not flogged and also pays. Rather he is only flogged, according to the principle in penal law that if a person is liable to both flogging and payment, he is not punished with both (see Hilchot Genevah 3:1).
and if he ate inadvertently. So he is not flogged, and therefore he pays for what he ate.
adds a fifth. He adds a fifth part equal to a quarter of the principal sum.
as we explained in Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah. Who falls into the category of zonah and chalalah, who are forbidden to a kohen; see there 18:3, 19:1.

like the law of any chalal. One whose father is a kohen and whose mother is unfit for the priesthood becomes a chalal and unfit for the priesthood, and this woman too was disqualified from the priesthood.
for a chalal is like a non-kohen in every respect. See Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 19:10.
with that which is set apart from holy offerings. What is separated from the offerings for the kohanim.

breast and thigh. Which are raised from the peace offering and given to the kohen. The same law applies to other parts of the offering that are given to the kohanim and eaten by their wives (see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 10:4-5, D.A.).
from the tradition they learned. On the basis of the Sages' tradition they interpreted the meaning of the verse.
but even a Levite woman or an Israelite woman, etc.. She too is included in the prohibition mentioned above, halacha 7.
even though she has a child from a kohen. And had she not been unchaste, she would have eaten terumah on account of her son, as below, halacha 12.

therefore a captive woman, etc.. The wife of a kohen who was taken captive by gentiles is disqualified from the priesthood out of concern that they had relations with her (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 18:17-23).
even though she says, 'I am pure'. For she is not believed to testify about herself that she was not violated.

and any captive woman who is believed to say 'I am pure'. For example, where we know only from her that she was taken captive, in which case she is believed to say that she is pure (there, halacha 21).
or who has a witness. One witness who testifies that she is pure, for in this matter they were lenient to rely on one witness (there, halacha 17).
so that she may be permitted to her husband, she may eat terumah. If this is testimony sufficient to permit her to her husband the kohen, she may also eat terumah.
and a woman who was subjected to bestiality has not been disqualified from the priesthood. Since she is not included in the category of zonah (there, halacha 1).
12-13. she eats on account of her son. Even if she is no longer married to a kohen and cannot eat by virtue of the marriage.
tumtum. One whose reproductive organs are covered and it is not discernible whether he is male or female. [Note: In his Commentary on the Mishnah, Maimonides vocalizes this word: tumtom.]
and androgynos. One who has both male and female reproductive organs (see Hilchot Ishut 2:24-25).
and even a child's child. Even if her son or daughter from the kohen died and left offspring, she may eat terumah as long as she has any offspring at all from the kohen.

and she has no child, just as the child of an Israelite, etc.. This verse was stated regarding the terumah-eating of a kohen's daughter who married an Israelite, and the Sages derived from it that the terumah-eating of a kohen's wife also depends on the child she has from her husband.
and one with whom she may not have relations had relations with the daughter, or she married a mamzer, etc.. In both of these cases the child is a mamzer (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:1).
and even an Israelite. Since a mamzer is forbidden to enter the congregation of Israel.
and needless to say if she had a daughter from a kohen, etc.. For she was born a kohenet.
even if she was profaned. For example, a kohen had relations with her while she was divorced.
similarly a kohen's daughter. Who married an Israelite.
even though his mother has died. And only the kohen's daughter and her grandchild remain, and both are kohanim.

and this one says: 'Not like the sons of the High Priest, who disqualifies me from terumah'. The kohen's daughter says that there should not be many like him, even though he is a High Priest, since he disqualifies her from terumah. And 'like the sons of' is not precise, but rather 'son of my son' (Meiri, Yevamot 67b).
a slave does not disqualify. The kohen's daughter from terumah.
and does not enable to eat. Does not enable a kohen's wife to eat terumah.
and he had relations with a maidservant and she bore him a slave. He had relations with a Canaanite maidservant, and his offspring from her is a slave like her (Hilchot Avadim 9:1).
and the slave is still alive. And his father's mother has no other offspring.
for slaves have no lineage. They are not considered the children of their fathers (see Hilchot Ishut 15:6).
and he died and she has a son from him. And therefore she continued to eat terumah.
she may not eat terumah. Although she has a son from the kohen, since now she is married to an Israelite.
if the Israelite died and she has a son from him, she may not eat terumah. Although she has a son from the kohen, because we follow the last one.
and she returned and married a kohen, she may eat terumah. According to her present status.
he died and she has a son from him, she may eat terumah. Like the law of an Israelite woman who has offspring from a kohen, who does not revert to the status of an Israelite.
and she may not eat of the breast and thigh. As above, halacha 7.
and she returned and married a kohen, she may eat terumah. According to her present status, like the law of an Israelite woman who is married to a kohen.

'any man of the offspring of Aaron who is a leper or has a discharge'. And likewise other impurities, as explained in the continuation of the passage and as expounded in the Sifra (Emor, parashah 4, chapter 4, halacha 4).
you say, terumot. Unlike the most holy offerings, which only male kohanim may eat, and unlike lesser holy offerings, which she may not eat after she was divorced or widowed.
as it is said, 'They shall keep my charge, lest they bear sin for it'. And the continuation of the verse: 'and die for it if they profane it.'

and an impure person who ate pure terumah, although it is a prohibition, is not flogged, for it is not holy. The prohibition is stated generally and includes impure terumah, but the punishment is stated only regarding eating that profanes the holy, whereas impure terumah is already profaned since it became impure.
impure persons may not eat terumah until, etc.. A kohen who became impure and immersed, his purification is not complete until the sun sets in the west and three medium stars are seen.
until the sky is clear of light. It is not enough for the sun to set; the sky must be dark and clear of its glow.
from something that is in its holiness. Holy things that did not become impure, for if they became impure they are not included in 'holy' (above, halacha 1).

and a prohibition that comes from a general positive commandment is a positive commandment. A prohibition derived from the general form of a positive commandment is not considered a negative prohibition but a positive commandment.
to emit semen. And if it emerges he will be impure and would eat terumah while impure.

holds the member. He grips his organ with his hand to prevent the emission of semen (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Niddah 5:2), for he does not become impure until the semen emerges (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 5:1).
the imbecile and the deaf-mute. Who are kohanim, and became impure.

for if they sleep they are impure. There is concern that they will become impure through a seminal emission, and because of lack of understanding they will not treat themselves as impure (see Riko, below, halacha 6).
unless they made them a copper pouch. To cover the member, and after they get up it can be checked whether the pouch is clean.
because of the heat of riding. From the friction against the camel's skin.

a woman who had relations... immerses and eats terumah in the evening. According to the law of a man and woman who had relations, who become impure with the impurity of seminal emission (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 5:9).

if she did not turn over during intercourse, etc.. But remained lying on her back, in which case the semen is absorbed and there is no concern that it will emerge from her afterward. If she turned over, it is not absorbed and emerges within three days.
as will be explained in its place. There, 5:11.

since its basis is rabbinic. For by strict law one does not separate from produce of outside the Land, and the Sages ordained separation in some places (above 1:1; and see also Hilchot Bikkurim 5:10-11, a similar law regarding challah outside the Land).
those who have seen a seminal emission. People who have had a seminal emission.
and all of them, etc.. Even for these, from whose bodies impurity issues, the Sages were lenient that they need not wait after they immerse until the evening.
those impure by contact with impurities. Who became impure because they touched something that causes impurity.
for we cannot be purified from it today. Because the purification process requires sprinkling of water mixed with the ashes of the red heifer, and today we have no ashes of a red heifer.
whether he touched a creeping creature. From which impurity he can be purified through immersion.
and a minor girl who has not yet seen menstrual blood. No blood that causes menstrual impurity has come from her.
and a leper is like one from whose body impurity issues. Although the impurity is in his skin, outside his body, nevertheless he is impure because of his body and not because of contact.

provided that a kohen of established lineage declares him impure. For the impurity of a leper is determined only by a kohen (Hilchot Tum'at Tzara'at 9:2; for the definition of a kohen of established lineage see above 6:2).
at the Pesach. In eating the Pesach offering.

just as the resident and hired worker mentioned regarding the Pesach, etc.. Regarding the Pesach offering the Torah says explicitly that an uncircumcised man may not eat it (Exodus 12:48). And the Sages learned by gezerah shavah that the same applies to eating terumah, in which too the words 'resident and hired worker' appear.

mashuch (one whose foreskin has been drawn forward). In circumcision the skin of the foreskin is cut and the tip of the organ is exposed down to below the corona; 'mashuch' is a state in which after the circumcision the skin of the organ has returned and covered the tip so that he does not look circumcised.

and by rabbinic decree he must circumcise, etc.. By rabbinic law he is forbidden to eat until he is circumcised (Sefer HaMitzvot, negative commandment 135, and so explained the Arukh HaShulchan 74:6; the Riko and Radbaz explain that a mashuch is permitted to eat terumah, but he needs a second circumcision by rabbinic law).
that he must circumcise a second time. See Hilchot Milah 2:5.
and one born circumcised. Born without a foreskin.
may eat terumah. Although he is obligated in the drawing of covenantal blood (see Hilchot Milah 1:7).
their wives and their slaves may eat. For they are fit kohanim who are merely prevented from eating for various reasons.

one with crushed testicles or severed organ. A man whose testicles were crushed or whose member was cut off by human hands, who is forbidden to enter the congregation and to marry an Israelite woman (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah chapter 16).
but their wives may not eat. Since she is forbidden to him, he disqualified her from terumah, as with a zonah (see there 18:3 and above 6:10).
if he had not known his wife... these may eat. Since she was not disqualified by intercourse.

and likewise if he married a daughter of converts, she may eat. Since those unfit for the congregation are permitted to converts, her status is that of a fit kohen's wife (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 16:1).

a kohen with crushed testicles who betrothed a kohen's daughter, she may not eat. From her father's house's terumah; although she has not yet been disqualified by a forbidden union, the Sages disqualified her because of her betrothal, which designates her for a forbidden union when she marries (as below, halacha 21).

sris chamah (one born a eunuch). One born with a defect in development who is unable to father children. Since he was born so, he is not included in 'crushed testicles or severed organ' (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 16:9).
the slaves of an androgynos and a tumtum may eat. Since every kohen enables his slaves to eat, regardless of his gender, for even the slaves of a kohen's daughter are permitted terumah.
but not their wives. Since they are not definitely male, their kiddushin is also in doubt, and their wives do not have the status of a kohen's wife.
a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor. Who are kohanim.

who bought slaves for themselves, they may not eat. This refers to their buying themselves, and since they lack sufficient understanding their purchase has no validity and these are not their slaves (see Hilchot Mechirah 29:1).
but if the court bought for them... these may eat. Since others acquire and bring it into their ownership.
the court or the trustees. Those responsible for the property of orphans (see Hilchot Nachalot 10:5).

for one unfit for terumah. In some versions: 'for one who disqualifies from terumah,' and that seems the main reading (see R. Y. Shilat in his notes to the Mishneh Torah Mugah), namely one who is forbidden to her and whose relations disqualify her from terumah (above 6:1).
in the manner of his maleness. Anally, which is the act that is done in male homosexual relations.

he is disqualified from eating terumah like women. Perhaps he is a woman, whose law is that if she had relations with one forbidden to her, she may not eat terumah because she becomes a zonah (above 6:10), whether through natural or unnatural intercourse (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 18:6).

but in the manner of his maleness, a male does not disqualify a male from the priesthood. The commentators had difficulty with Maimonides' words, since at the beginning of the halacha he wrote that a male disqualifies him even in the manner of his maleness, so that a male disqualifies a male from the priesthood; see the Riko, Radbaz and Yad Peshutah.
where one of them does not enable eating. For example, where one of the partners is an Israelite and his slaves are not permitted terumah.
this slave is forbidden to eat. For he is not the acquisition of a kohen alone, and the Torah says of him, 'if a kohen buys a person as his property,' meaning that he must belong entirely to a kohen.
and she brought him in. She brought him with her from her father's house.

melog slaves. Slaves who are part of the 'melog' property (usufruct property), which remains in the wife's possession during the marriage. They eat terumah by virtue of her, and she eats by virtue of her husband.

tzon barzel slaves. Slaves who are part of the 'tzon barzel' property (iron-flock property), which passes during the marriage into the husband's possession, and they eat terumah by virtue of the husband (for an explanation of these terms see Hilchot Ishut 16:1-2).
even the acquisition of the acquisition may eat. Not only the person whom the kohen bought is permitted terumah, but also the property acquired by the person he bought (Riko).
and an acquisition that eats enables to eat, etc.. Only an acquisition that is permitted to eat himself can enable his own acquisition to eat.
these may not eat. Since they now belong to a man and woman who are not permitted terumah.
a widow to a High Priest, a divorcee or a chalutzah to an ordinary kohen. Who are forbidden to marry them by a negative prohibition (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:1).
and likewise other women forbidden by negative commandments. Whose marriage the Torah forbade by a negative commandment, and she is disqualified from terumah like a zonah (as above 6:7).
melog slaves may not eat, even though he is obligated for their maintenance. Since they are hers and she is forbidden terumah.
he married a secondary relation. A woman forbidden to him on account of 'sheniyot,' which are forbidden relations prohibited by rabbinic law and not by the Torah (Hilchot Ishut 1:6).
she may eat. For the Sages did not disqualify her as a zonah (there 18:4).

but her melog slaves may not eat. The Sages ruled that they may not eat, although she herself eats (later authorities had difficulty with the reason; see the Arukh HaShulchan 75:11, who wrote that they penalized her so that she would know that her marriage is a forbidden one), but tzon barzel slaves eat by virtue of her husband.
a kohen's daughter, a widow... or a divorcee. Who eats terumah before her marriage by virtue of her father's house (above 6:8).
designated. Set aside.
for a disqualifying union. When they marry.

and likewise if they entered the chuppah without betrothal, etc.. Chuppah is the couple's being alone together for the purpose of marriage (see Hilchot Ishut 10:1). Ordinarily seclusion alone has no validity if it was not preceded by an act of kiddushin, but here the Sages disqualified her from terumah because chuppah is close to intercourse (Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 57-58).
they may not eat. Even if he did not have relations with her.
from the betrothal they returned to their fitness and eat. For they were not disqualified but only temporarily forbidden.
for they have already been profaned. By intercourse.
a kohen's daughter whose husband, a kohen, died. Without children.
and she fell before brothers-in-law among whom is a chalal. One of her husband's brothers who are supposed to perform levirate marriage with her is a chalal who may not eat terumah.

because of the bond of the chalal. The widow has a certain marital bond with all the brothers because of the commandment of levirate marriage, and when one of them is a chalal he prevents her from eating terumah, as with the wife of a chalal.

ma'amar (levirate betrothal). A rabbinic enactment that the brother-in-law betroths his sister-in-law with money before he has relations with her for the purpose of levirate marriage. This kiddushin is called 'ma'amar' (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 2:1).
for a ma'amar does not completely acquire the yevamah. Rather only intercourse does, and since she is not entirely his wife, she still has a connection to the other brothers, including the chalal.
a kohen who gave a get to his yevamah, a kohenet. A kohen's daughter whose husband, a kohen, died, and his brother, a kohen, gave her a get instead of levirate marriage or chalitzah.

for she became forbidden to him but his bond to her still remains. The commandment of levirate marriage is still in force, but it is forbidden for him to marry her by rabbinic law because of the get (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 5:1), and thus she is designated for a rabbinically disqualifying union.
she may eat terumah. Because she is a kohenet.

because she is designated for a disqualifying union of rabbinic origin. And not for a union forbidden by the Torah; only if she is designated for a union forbidden by the Torah did they forbid her to eat terumah.

and likewise a kohenet who is a chalutzah or a secondary relation who was betrothed to a kohen may eat. Since a chalutzah and a secondary relation are forbidden to a kohen by rabbinic law and are not designated for a union forbidden by the Torah (see there 1:12).
an ailonit. A woman with defective sexual development, who is unable to bear children.

she may eat terumah. Although a person who has not fulfilled the commandment to be fruitful and multiply may not marry her (Hilchot Ishut 15:7), she does not become a zonah and is not disqualified from terumah, for this is not an intrinsic prohibition (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 18:3).
disqualify. From eating terumah.
and do not enable to eat. They do not give the right to eat terumah even though they are kohanim.

an Israelite woman pregnant by a kohen, etc.. But she is not married to a kohen and therefore does not eat by virtue of him, whereas the fetus who will be a kohen will enable her to eat terumah only once born (above 6:12).

and a kohen's daughter pregnant by an Israelite is forbidden to eat... 'as in her youth,' excluding a pregnant woman. Although she is not married to him, she does not eat by virtue of her father's house, since she is pregnant, and is not as she was in her youth (Radbaz, following Rashi).
a kohen's daughter with whom an Israelite had relations. Illicit relations, without marriage.

we do not suspect that perhaps she became pregnant. For if she became pregnant, the fetus disqualifies her from terumah. And even if it later becomes clear that she was pregnant and she will be disqualified from terumah, nevertheless her eating in the meantime will not count as forbidden eating, since she did not have to be concerned about pregnancy.
rather she immerses, etc.. From the impurity of seminal emission caused by marital relations (as above 7:7).

she was married to an Israelite and her husband died, she immerses and eats terumah in the evening until forty days. In marriage there is greater concern of pregnancy than with illicit relations, and therefore she eats only until forty days, because until then it is not yet considered a pregnancy, as explained below.

and if her pregnancy became known, she is retroactively spoiled. If she continued to eat after the forty days, and afterward it became clear that she was pregnant, everything she ate from the fortieth day onward counts as inadvertent eating of terumah (Riko).
for during all forty days it is not a fetus but is considered mere water. See Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:1.
an Israelite woman who married a kohen and he died. And after his death she and her slaves are permitted terumah if she has a son from him.
and left her pregnant. And there were no other children by whose virtue they could eat.

her slaves may not eat terumah on account of the fetus, for the one who is born is the one who enables eating. Since the son confers the right to terumah only after he is born, and just as she is forbidden terumah, so are her slaves.
therefore, etc.. Since the fetus is not taken into account, this has an implication also for slaves whom the father bequeathed to his sons, who can eat by virtue of being a kohen's slaves.
if the fetus was a chalal. Unfit for the priesthood, and when born he will not be a kohen, and his slaves also will not eat.
rather they eat on account of his fit brothers. If there are other sons fit for the priesthood, the slaves can eat on their account, since the fetus is not taken into account.
until this chalal is born and the slaves are forbidden to eat. When he is born he is also taken into account, and their law is that of slaves of partners, one of whom is not a kohen (above 7:17).
how is it with a yavam?. He disqualifies and does not enable to eat.
an Israelite woman bound to a kohen yavam. Whose husband died, and therefore she no longer eats by virtue of him and is bound to her husband's brother because of the commandment of levirate marriage.
excluding one who awaits a yavam. Who is still bound to her husband's house.
or he had partial relations with her and did not complete. His act of intercourse.
as we explained in Hilchot Yibbum. Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 2:3.
until he has complete, willing intercourse. That is intercourse that is also effective for the acquisition of an ordinary wife.

where she was widowed from betrothal. Although one who performs levirate marriage with his brother's betrothed has her as his wife in every form of intercourse, since she did not eat beforehand (for a betrothed woman does not eat terumah, above 6:3), they were strict that she may not eat until he has intercourse that is also effective for the kiddushin of an ordinary wife.
for he has acquisition in her. The acquisition of kiddushin, which disqualifies her from terumah.
lest she feed the members of her father's house. But by strict law she is permitted terumah since he has an acquisition in her.
as we explained. Above 6:3.
for she is not yet betrothed. Because the kiddushin will take effect only after thirty days.
from now, after thirty days, she is forbidden to eat immediately. For it is possible that she is betrothed retroactively already from now (see Hilchot Ishut 7:12 and Maggid Mishneh there).
and likewise with all other conditions of this kind. See Hilchot Ishut chapter 7.
the deaf-mute. That is, a deaf-mute (Hilchot Ishut 2:26). And although he has no understanding and cannot betroth by Torah law, the Sages instituted kiddushin for him (there 4:9).
for he acquires by rabbinic enactment. Therefore she is forbidden terumah because of her marriage to him.
and an Israelite woman who married a deaf kohen may not eat, for he does not acquire by Torah law. And since she is not his wife by Torah law, she does not eat terumah by virtue of him.

she was betrothed to a hearing kohen and he did not manage to marry her before he became deaf, she may not eat. Although she is his wife, they decreed that she may not eat, lest people err to permit her terumah also in the kiddushin of a deaf man, which is not valid (Riko, following the Gemara).

he died and she fell before a deaf yavam and he performed levirate marriage with her, she may not eat. Although levirate marriage by a deaf man is valid by Torah law (Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 6:3), since she did not eat when he was hearing (for a betrothed woman does not eat), she may not eat after the levirate marriage (similar to above, halacha 7).
she may eat, since she was eating originally. And she also entered levirate marriage properly.

and the wife of a deaf man who bore a child from him may eat on account of her son. Although her marriage is not valid, since she has offspring from a kohen she is permitted terumah (as below, halacha 14).
since his intercourse is intercourse. For from this age his intercourse counts (see Hilchot Ishut 11:3).
as we explained. Above 6:10.

even if he was shachuf. A man who cannot become erect and father children; although this is not intercourse by Torah law, the woman is disqualified from terumah by rabbinic law (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:11).

she may not eat on account of the minor because he does not acquire. Although she married him and his intercourse is intercourse, she is not like the wife of a kohen who is permitted terumah, since the marriage of a minor has no validity.

because he does not acquire until he grows up. Unlike intercourse, which depends on physical ability, kiddushin also depends on understanding, and he acquires only when he is thirteen years and a day and has brought signs of maturity (see Hilchot Ishut 2:10, 4:7).
a doubt whether he is nine years old. An unfit person who had relations with a woman, and there is doubt whether he was already nine, the age at which his intercourse disqualifies.
two hairs. The signs of maturity in his body that are required (in addition to the age of thirteen years and a day) for him to be considered an adult.
she is forbidden to eat. For in both cases the doubt is resolved stringently.
with terumah of rabbinic origin. Cases in which the Sages required separating terumah.
and these do not disqualify. From eating terumah by intercourse.
and do not enable to eat. And the woman with whom they have relations does not eat terumah.
the rapist and the seducer. One who has relations with a virgin girl by force or who seduced a minor (Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:2).
and the imbecile who married a woman. Whose kiddushin has no validity even rabbinically (unlike a deaf-mute).
as we explained. Above 6:10.
she eats on account of her son. Although she was not married to his father, it is enough that her son is a kohen.

and although the matter is doubtful, etc.. Although it is not certain that the kohen is his father, since she was not married to him and she may have conceived from another; only for a married woman are her children presumed to be her husband's (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 15:20).

provided that no rumor went out about her, etc.. This permission is on condition that no rumor spread that she had a relationship with another man, but all gossip about her only on account of the kohen.
she may not eat because of the fetus. For a fetus disqualifies from terumah, as above, halacha 1.
the fetus was cut up. And died while she was pregnant.

witnesses of warning and witnesses of seclusion. Witnesses that her husband warned her not to be alone with a particular man, and witnesses that she did in fact go into seclusion and was alone with him. She drinks the bitter waters in the Temple to determine whether she was unfaithful, and in the meantime she is forbidden to her husband (for details see Hilchot Sotah chapter 1).
because she is a possible zonah. Out of concern for relations with a man not her husband, which disqualifies her as a zonah, she is forbidden terumah because of the doubt.
until she drinks the bitter waters. And it will be determined whether she was unfaithful, and if it becomes clear that she was not unfaithful she is permitted terumah.
or she was one of the women who do not drink, etc.. For example, where one witness came and testified that she was unfaithful with the man her husband warned her about (see Hilchot Sotah 1:14-15).
she is forbidden terumah forever. Since she did not drink she remains a possible zonah.
I am impure. That she had relations with another man, and according to her words she is disqualified because she has the status of a zonah.
a minor girl. Who is betrothed and married only with her father's consent (Hilchot Ishut 3:13).
whether in her father's presence. And he was silent.
or not in his presence. And there is concern that he does not agree to it.
even though her father betrothed her. And only the marriage, that is the chuppah, was done without his knowledge.

for if he protests she is retroactively a stranger. If he protests the marriage she reverts retroactively to being betrothed and forbidden terumah (above 6:3), and it turns out that in the meantime she ate terumah illicitly.

and as for one who sees and is silent, he is angry. Although he saw that she married and was silent, this is no proof that he agreed, for perhaps he was silent because he was angry that she married without his knowledge, and perhaps in the future he will protest (see also Hilchot Ishut 22:5).
the woman. The wife of a kohen, who eats terumah by virtue of him.
until the get reaches her hand. And from that moment she is divorced and does not eat by virtue of her husband.
her agent whom she made for receipt. An agent on her behalf who receives the get for her, and when the get reaches his hand she is divorced as if it had reached her hand (Hilchot Gerushin 6:1).
and any woman about whom there is doubt whether she is divorced. There is doubt whether her divorce is valid.
she may not eat. Out of concern that the divorce is valid and she is no longer a kohen's wife.
who made an agent. Appointed an agent.
she is forbidden to eat terumah immediately. Perhaps he received the get immediately after she appointed him as agent.

and if she said to him, 'Receive my get for me in such-and-such place'. She appointed him to receive the get in a particular place, and she is not divorced if he received it in another place (Hilchot Gerushin 9:34).

she is forbidden only until the agent reaches that place. She is forbidden only after the time needed for the agent to reach that place has passed, for only then is there concern that he has already received the get for her.

she sent an agent to bring her get. This is a different kind of agent, who does not receive the get on her behalf but only brings it to her, and she is divorced when the get reaches her hand (there 6:4-5).
one who says to his wife, etc.. He gave her the get and stipulated that it take effect only an hour before he dies.
she is forbidden to eat terumah immediately. Perhaps he will die in an hour, and it is possible that she is already divorced.
a city surrounded by a karkom. An army that besieged it.
and a ship tossed at sea. That was caught in a storm.
and one who goes out to be judged. To stand trial, and perhaps a death sentence will be pronounced against him.
sails. Sails out in a ship.
and goes out with a caravan. That travels from place to place and may be in danger.
but a city captured by a karkom. Whose way is to kill its inhabitants.
and a ship that was lost at sea. So that no possibility remained of saving it (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Gittin 3:4).
and one who goes out to be executed by gentile courts. A death sentence was pronounced against him, but the court may retract its sentence.

we apply to them the stringencies of the dead and the stringencies of the living. We are concerned and are strict according to both possibilities, perhaps he is alive and perhaps dead (see also Hilchot Gerushin 6:28-29).

but one whose sentence was finalized in a Jewish court. Who committed a transgression for which death is the penalty. And the liability to death does not depend on the court's will but is by the Torah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Arachin 1:3).
at the place of stoning. The place where the punishment of stoning is carried out.
he is presumed dead and his wife may not eat. And if he is an Israelite and his wife a kohen's daughter, she is permitted terumah since he surely died (Kesef Mishneh, and see D.A.).
they left her husband dying in another country. If he was about to die when the witnesses left there.

for most dying people die. And therefore an Israelite woman, the wife of a kohen, may not eat, lest her husband has died, and on the other hand a kohen's daughter, the wife of an Israelite, may not eat, since there is no certainty that he has already died.
one says. One witness.

she may not eat. Out of doubt, perhaps he died and perhaps he did not die. But if one witness came and testified that he died, he is believed to permit her to remarry, even if he is someone who is ordinarily unfit to testify (see Hilchot Gerushin 12:15). And consequently, if she is a kohen's daughter she is permitted terumah.

her co-wife or one of the five women told her, etc.. Anyone is fit to testify that her husband died, except for five female relatives who are not believed out of concern that they want to harm her (see Hilchot Gerushin 12:15-16).

since she may not remarry on their word, she eats terumah on the presumption that her husband is alive. Just as her husband is presumed alive with regard to her being forbidden to remarry and their testimony is not believed, so he is presumed alive with regard to eating terumah.
one who frees his slave, etc.. A Canaanite slave, who is freed by his master through a document (shtar) of release.
once it is acquired for him. Through another person who receives the document on his behalf, whereby the slave is freed (see Hilchot Avadim 6:1).
and any slave who went out to freedom but is still held back from release. There are several cases in which he goes out to freedom but still needs a document of release to be fully freed.
as will be explained in Hilchot Avadim. Chapter 8.
nevertheless he is forbidden to eat terumah. Since he is no longer entirely his money's acquisition (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 42b).

one who writes his property to another and it is acquired for him through someone else. He wrote on his own initiative a deed of gift to his fellow of all his property, and transferred it to him by giving the deed to someone who would acquire it on his behalf. A person can transfer to his fellow something to his benefit since presumably he agrees to it, unless he protests and it becomes clear that he did not agree.
and there were slaves among them. Among the property he gave him.
and the one to whom they were given was silent. From his silence it can be understood that he agreed to receive the gift.
and afterward cried out. He protested and did not agree to acquire them.
the end proved about the beginning. The protest at the end shows that the silence at the beginning should not be interpreted as agreement, and the acquisition is not valid.

or this one who cried out after being silent changed his mind. For at first he agreed and therefore was silent and acquired, and only afterward changed his mind and therefore protested, and since he acquired the moment he was silent, the acquisition can no longer be canceled.
therefore they may not eat terumah, etc.. Since there is doubt whether the second acquired them and to whom they belong.
their master. Their lord.
he feeds it terumah. Like the law of a kohen's animal, which eats terumah.
because it is not the acquisition of his money. Of the renter, but of the lessor.

an Israelite who put a cow with a kohen to fatten it, with the profit shared between them. They made an agreement by which the Israelite buys a cow from a kohen in order to fatten and sell it, and does not pay him immediately; rather he assesses its value and it remains a debt on him for the time being, and after he fattens and sells it, he pays the kohen the debt and also half of the profit that came from the fattening.
although the kohen has a share in its increase. Since its body already belongs to the Israelite.
for he assumed it upon himself. He assessed its value and it is a debt on him and it is acquired by him.

for the firstborn belongs to the kohanim. The firstborn belongs to the kohanim even before it is given to them (and see Minchat Chinuch, commandment 80, that this law applies only to a blemished firstborn).
and a person stores karshinei (bitter vetch). He gathers legumes that are animal food.

for by Torah law money acquires. By Torah law it already belongs to the Israelite, because payment of money constitutes acquisition, but the Sages ordained that payment alone does not acquire movable property, but only an act of acquisition such as pulling.
as will be explained in Hilchot Mekach UMimkar. Hilchot Mechirah 3:1-5.
even if he gave the money, she may not eat terumah until he pulls. Since by rabbinic law it is not yet the kohen's.
a non-kohen. One who is forbidden to eat terumah.
principal. The value of the terumah he ate.
and a fifth. And he adds a further quarter of the value of the terumah, which is a fifth of the total final payment (below, halacha 26, and Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 6:1).
but did not know whether he is liable to death for it. Death at the hand of Heaven for deliberate eating (above 6:6).
it is inadvertent. He is not considered deliberate until he also knows its punishment (see Hilchot Shegagot 2:2).
that it is normally eaten. For if it is not normally eaten, he is exempt from the fifth and pays only the principal, and likewise regarding drinking and anointing (see below, halachot 7-8, 11).
one who anoints. On his skin, a liquid produced from terumah such as oil.

as it is said, 'and they shall not profane...' to include one who anoints. This prohibition is stated after the prohibition of a non-kohen eating terumah, and the Sages learned that it comes to add also anointing with terumah.
he is not liable for the fifth until he eats the volume of an olive. But he is liable for the principal even for less.
as it is said. Regarding liability for the fifth.
within the time of eating a peras. The time it takes to eat half a loaf of bread, whose measure is three eggs (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 14:8-9).
within the time of drinking a revi'it. A quarter of a log.

these combine to the volume of an olive. If he ate or drank an olive's volume within this time, it counts as one act of eating or drinking and he is liable for it, but if over a longer time, they count as two acts of eating or drinking, in none of which is there an olive's volume.
and terumat ma'aser... of demai. Which was separated from produce that is obligated in separation out of doubt (Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1).
to make him liable to death for them. This detail does not refer to terumat ma'aser of demai, since it is not from the Torah (Riko, Kesef Mishneh).
for all of them are called terumah. In the Torah (see Numbers 15:19, Deuteronomy 12:17).

just as one is not liable for the fifth on his own second tithe. When redeeming second tithe one must add a fifth of its value, and with demai produce the Sages exempted him from this, lest if they obligated him in the fifth he would eat without redeeming at all (Jerusalem Talmud, Demai 1:2).
as will be explained. Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 5:4.
but the Sages said, etc.. Regarding the eating of demai terumah the Sages thought the opposite, that if they exempted him from the fifth, they would come to treat it lightly.
they would treat it lightly. And would not treat demai terumah as holy (Jerusalem Talmud there).
if they warned him. They cautioned him before eating that it is forbidden and that he will be punished if he eats.
he is flogged and does not pay. For one is not liable to both flogging and payment; see above 6:6.
and does not pay the fifth. For liability for the fifth is stated only regarding inadvertent eating (Leviticus 22:14).
he pays the value of wood. As its worth as fuel.
because it is fit only for burning. Like the law of impure terumah (below 12:1), and its value is determined accordingly.
terumah that is chametz. Terumah that is leavened, for example if he ate on Pesach bread prepared from terumah wheat.
even if he separated it when it was matzah. Before it leavened. For if he separated it after it leavened, the separation has no validity and it is not terumah (Radbaz).

for it is not fit for burning because it is forbidden for benefit, it has no value. Chametz is forbidden even for benefit and it is forbidden even to burn it (see Hilchot Chametz UMatzah 3:11), and therefore when he ate it, it was worthless and he need not pay.

one who inadvertently ate terumah on Yom Kippur. Although for eating on Yom Kippur he is liable to karet, this is no reason to exempt him from payment, for only liability to the death penalty by a court exempts from payment (even inadvertently, see Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:11-14).

or ate pecked-at terumah. Terumah produce that was pecked at by animals, and is forbidden to eat out of concern for danger and must be discarded (see below 12:13). And although it is not meant for eating, he must pay principal and fifth.
and one who drinks terumah wine that was left uncovered. For this too is forbidden because of the danger and must be poured out (there).
and one who anoints with wine and oil as one. Although people do not usually anoint with wine, since people usually anoint with oil, he is liable also for the wine (Radbaz).
or one who drank oil and vinegar as one. Although people do not usually drink oil, since people usually drink vinegar, he is liable also for the oil (Arukh HaShulchan 79:19).
or who chewed raw wheat or gulped vinegar. He ate wheat kernels raw or drank vinegar. Although this is not the accepted way of eating, there are those who eat this way.
and he was disgusted by his food. He does not want to eat any more.
not that he should harm himself. And eating in such a manner is considered as if he ate foods that are not fit to eat (see Hilchot Shevitat Asor 2:7).
the barley. Which is animal food.
jujubes. A cultivated jujube whose fruits are small and round or elongated.
and vomited them. Whole.
and the second pays the value of wood. Since after the vomiting they were fit for burning and not for eating.
to the first. Since the first one enjoyed eating the jujubes and became liable for their value, they are his.
one who feeds his workers and his guests terumah. And they did not know that it is terumah.
and he pays them. If he was obligated to feed them (Melechet Shlomo, Terumot 6:3).

the value of their meal, etc.. Since a person recoils from eating forbidden food and does not enjoy eating it, it is as if he did not feed them, and he must pay them the value of the meal, and he pays them according to the value of the chullin produce he was supposed to feed them, which is more expensive than terumah produce (Radbaz, and see the Riko and Arukh HaShulchan 79:23).

one who feeds his minor children. Who are not commanded not to eat terumah. And their father pays on their behalf, for he caused the kohen a loss. But since he did not eat the terumah himself, he pays only the principal and not the fifth.

and his slaves, whether adults or minors. Canaanite slaves. And even an adult slave is exempt, since his property belongs to his master and he has nothing to pay with. Therefore the householder pays, but only the principal.
and one who eats terumah of outside the Land. Whose obligation is rabbinic (above 1:6).
and one who eats or drinks less than an olive's volume. Who is not included in the liability for the fifth (above, halacha 2).

and a nazirite who inadvertently drank terumah wine. Since he is forbidden to drink wine, it is not considered drinking (see commentators who explained the distinction between the law here and the law of one who eats on Yom Kippur mentioned above, halacha 7).
and one who drinks oil. For drinking harms him (Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 35b).
and one who anoints with wine. For people do not do this.
a kohen's daughter who was married to an Israelite. And did not return to her father's house.
or who was disqualified. Who had relations with one forbidden to her (above 6:7).
pays the principal. Since she ate what belongs to the kohanim.
but does not pay the fifth. Since she is not entirely a stranger (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 7:2, following the Sifra).
a woman who had been eating terumah. The wife of a kohen.
the slave. A kohen's slave.
and left an heir who does not enable eating. The heir who inherited the slave is not one whose slaves eat terumah, for example, a chalal.
or gave you to him. Gave you to an Israelite as a gift.
freed you. And you became your own master, and are like a convert who is not a kohen.
and it became known that he is the son of a divorcee or the son of a chalutzah. That he is a chalal and does not have the status of a kohen.
these pay only the principal. And they are exempt from the fifth because they were presumed permitted terumah when they ate, and they owe the principal because they ate what belongs to the kohanim.
because its time is hurried. That it must be eaten before it becomes forbidden.
they hurried to eat and did not check. And they are exempt also from the principal because this is complete duress (Arukh HaShulchan 79:27).
these must spit it out. They must spit it out of their mouths.
you became impure or the terumah became impure. Now.
you were impure or the terumah was impure. Before you began to eat.
or it became known that it is tevel, etc.. These laws apply to any person who was eating and learned that he put into his mouth something forbidden to eat.

or he tasted the taste of a bedbug in his mouth. This speaks of a kohen who ate terumah and felt in his mouth the taste of a bedbug. They permitted him to spit out the food in his mouth because of the revulsion caused by the taste of the bedbug, and did not worry about the loss of the terumah (following the Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 8:2).
baskets. Baskets.

I say it fell into the terumah one. One may be lenient and assume that the terumah fell into the basket containing terumah, and their status did not change (in rabbinic terumah only; see below 13:14).
and it is not known which is the terumah one. If there are two baskets, one of chullin and one of terumah, and it is not known which basket holds the terumah, and he ate from one of them.
for the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from his fellow. And one cannot obligate payment on the basis of doubt.
and the second. The second basket, from which he did not eat.
treat it as terumah. One must be strict with it out of doubt.
if another ate the second, he too is exempt. For from his standpoint too one can argue that the burden of proof is on the claimant, perhaps the basket he ate from is the chullin one.
one ate both of them. For he is certainly obligated to pay and the doubt is which of the two.
he pays like the smaller of the two. And not according to the larger, since there is no proof that he ate from the larger.
one who eats the fifth. Which he became liable for because he ate terumah, and the fifth becomes sanctified like terumah.
he adds a fifth to it. He must pay the fifth and add a fifth of it.

the payments are like terumah in every respect. One who eats terumah pays the kohen produce from which terumot and tithes have been separated (below, halacha 18). And in cases where he must pay principal and fifth, the produce has the law of terumah (it is permitted for eating only to a kohen, and the other laws of terumah apply), since the payment is called 'holy' in the Torah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 7:1).

except that if their growth was sown, it is chullin. What grows from the terumah produce that he sowed is considered chullin, unlike ordinary terumah, whose growth is forbidden to non-kohanim by rabbinic law (below 11:21).
and anyone who pays the principal. Only, and is exempt from the fifth.
an Israelite woman who ate terumah. And became liable for principal and fifth.
and afterward married a kohen. And her status is that of a kohenet, to whom principal and fifth may be paid.
if she ate terumah that no kohen had acquired. If she ate terumah that had not yet been given to a particular kohen.
she pays principal and fifth to herself. She separates rectified chullin produce, and takes it for herself, and it becomes terumah (as explained in the next halacha).
either way. Whether she ate terumah that a kohen had acquired or terumah that no kohen had acquired.

whether inadvertently or deliberately, he pays only from rectified chullin. He must pay in produce and cannot pay money, except that in the case of deliberate eating the produce does not become holy, and the kohen can waive the payment (above, halacha 15, and see Melechet Shlomo).
and they pay from leket, etc.. Which are exempt from terumah and are chullin that is rectified from the outset (above 2:10-11).
and from first tithe whose terumah was taken. Its terumat ma'aser.

even though the terumah gedolah in it has not yet been taken, if he put the tithe before the terumah. If he put first the first tithe from the ears before separating terumah gedolah from them, in which case he is exempt from the obligation of terumah gedolah (above 3:13, Kesef Mishneh; and see R. Akiva Eiger on Mishnah Terumot 6:5).

even though they were redeemed improperly. For example, second tithe that was redeemed with a piece of silver that is not a coin, or consecrated property that was redeemed with land (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 6:5, Kesef Mishneh; and the commentators on the Mishnah objected to this explanation, since in this manner the redemption has no validity at all, and therefore explained that this refers to cases where they were redeemed in a manner in which the redemption takes effect, but without adding the fifth).
and they pay from the new on behalf of the old. From this year's produce for eating terumah that was separated from produce of earlier years.
but they do not pay from one kind on behalf of another kind. From another type of fruit.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Shemittah 6:10.
his payments are payments. And they have the law of terumah (above, halacha 15).
and he must pay again from the pure. As a penalty (Babylonian Talmud, Gittin 54a).
the terumah of a chaver. Terumah belonging to a kohen who is careful about the laws of impurity and purity.
for pure items are not handed over to an am ha'aretz. Since what he pays becomes like terumah, and pure terumah is not given to an am ha'aretz; see above 6:2.
from his mother's father, a kohen. His grandfather is a kohen but he himself is not the son of a kohen.

and he ate it... does not pay himself. Since he ate the terumah inadvertently and became liable to pay the kohen, he cannot pay himself even after he inherited his grandfather, since he did not become a kohen (compare above, halacha 16).

rather he pays another heir from the rest of the tribe. He pays another heir of his mother's father, provided that he is a kohen, and he cannot give to any kohen, since the robbed property must be returned to the heirs of his grandfather.
it fell to him. By inheritance, and although it belongs to him in monetary terms, he cannot eat it (see Hilchot Ishut 5:6).
and the chaver gives them money. Since it belonged to them in monetary terms, except that they could not eat it themselves.

the money for which they would sell that terumah that they ate. Whose value is lower than chullin produce, since it may be eaten only by kohanim and must be eaten in purity; this is also called 'terumah money.'
he pays double payment to the owners. Like the law of a thief (Hilchot Genevah 4:1).
and he may pay it from terumah money. The double (compare above, halacha 18).
and ate it. Inadvertently.
he pays two principals and a fifth. Principal and fifth for the eating, and another principal as the double payment.
principal and fifth from chullin. Since he pays for eating terumah.
and principal even from terumah money. Since he pays double for the theft and not for the eating.
the terumah was consecrated. For example, the kohen consecrated the terumah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 6:4).
for the upkeep of the Temple. For repair of the Temple.
for there is no double payment for consecrated property. Only for one who steals from his fellow.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Genevah 2:1.
but he pays principal and two fifths. To the Temple treasury, which is the owner of the terumah.

and a fifth because he benefited from consecrated property. If he inadvertently benefited from consecrated property, he adds a fifth because he committed sacrilege against consecrated property (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:3).

if it contained the volume of an olive, etc.. Payment for terumah depends on eating an olive's volume and not on a particular value (above, halacha 2), whereas payment for sacrilege depends on having committed sacrilege with something worth a perutah (Hilchot Me'ilah there).

and if it is worth a perutah... he pays to the consecrated property. He pays the principal and two fifths to the Temple treasury: the principal because the terumah belongs to the Temple treasury, and also the fifth he pays for eating terumah follows it (Jerusalem Talmud, Terumot 6:2, and see Yad Peshutah).

and why does the prohibition of consecration apply to terumah?. For the rule is that a prohibition cannot take effect on a prior prohibition, whereas here the prohibition of sacrilege takes effect on the earlier prohibition of eating terumah.

therefore a prohibition is added on it also upon an Israelite. Since the second prohibition does not overlap with the first but adds to it, it can take effect on it, and an Israelite is liable for it on account of both.
in the manner that we explained in Hilchot Bi'ot Assurot. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 17:8.
and forbidden foods. Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 14:18.

one who steals terumah and eats it, etc.. A thief who swore falsely that he did not steal must return the stolen item and add a fifth (Hilchot Shevu'ot 1:8-9), and if he stole terumah, ate it and swore about it, by strict law he is liable for an additional fifth for eating terumah, but the Sages learned from the verse that he is liable for only one fifth.

for the holy he is liable only for the fifth of the holy alone. The fifth he is liable for on eating terumah, which is called 'holy,' and he does not pay another fifth with it (Arukh HaShulchan 80:18).
wherever we have said he pays principal and fifth, etc.. See also Hilchot Erchin VeCharamim 4:5.

if he ate the worth of four, he pays the worth of five of the kind he ate. For the fifth he adds is a quarter of the principal and is called a 'fifth' because it is a fifth of the final payment after calculating the principal and the fifth.
he pays the worth of six. Each fifth is calculated separately and is a fifth together with the principal.

for anointing is like drinking... and drinking is included in eating. Regarding terumah the Torah uses the language of eating several times (Leviticus 22), and the Sages interpreted that drinking is included in eating, and added, based on the verse in Psalms, that anointing is like drinking.
and this is what is called oil of burning. Since it has no other use except for lighting (and see its laws below, halachot 16-19).
it is permitted to crush them. To mash and stick them together.
the dried-fig cake. Figs stuck together.
and not autumn fruits. Grapes that ripen in the autumn season.
except for olives and grapes only. For wine and oil have special importance, and the way of growing olives and grapes is for pressing them.

he may drink it, and a non-kohen who ate, etc.. Although he changed them into a beverage they are not permitted to a non-kohen, but he is exempt from the fifth and from flogging, since he is liable only for eating, with respect to which the kohanim were commanded (Arukh HaShulchan 81:1).
he is not liable to pay. The fifth (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 11:2), but he is liable for the principal since he diminished the kohen's money (see above 10:11).
dried-fig cake. A lump of pressed figs.
and dried figs. Dried figs.
muries. A salty seasoning made from fish brine.
because it destroys them. Since it is customary to squeeze them after soaking and discard them, and terumah may not be destroyed (below 12:1).
but one may put wine into muries. In order to improve its taste, for the wine itself is used for eating (Riko).
and one does not perfume the oil, etc.. He should not add fragrances and the like that turn it into a medicinal ointment, because this takes it out of the category of food.
but one may mix wine, etc.. It is permitted to mix oil, wine and spices for the purpose of eating.
because it diminishes it. In quantity, although the cooking adds to it taste and aroma (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 11:1).
one does not mix grain with legumes. Since grain is more important and the very mixing of it into a majority of legumes constitutes a loss of it (Radbaz).
and anything that will separate from the other when sifted. That the kinds can be separated with a sieve.

and after the land of Judah was destroyed they began to mix grain with grain and legumes with legumes. After the destruction, because of poverty they were not careful about mixing in chullin, and therefore they permitted doing so also with terumah (there).
that they sift. Sifting is one of the stages of sifting flour from refuse.
and throws away the bran. The coarse refuse of the grain that remains mixed in the flour, and bran is not eaten by itself (and see halacha 12).
to make fine flour sifted many times. To sift the flour many times to make it clean fine flour.
until he removes a kav or two kavs from the se'ah. A kav is a sixth of a se'ah.
the rest. Which is less fine flour.
because it is fit for eating. And throwing it away is a loss of terumah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 11:5).
one does not seal an oven or stove with it. It is forbidden to smear it on a new oven or stove to strengthen them.
and one does not anoint a shoe or sandal with it. To soften them.
but he may anoint his foot and put on the shoe or sandal. And they soften anyway from the oil on his foot.
and rolls. Lies and turns himself from side to side.
a katavolia. A leather mat used for lying.
new. That needs softening.
and although they are anointed, he need not worry. Since he already anointed it on his body (and see below, halachot 8-9; and see also Hilchot Shemittah 5:7).

he may not put oil on a marble slab to roll on it, because he destroys it. Even when he puts it on a marble slab that absorbs nothing it is forbidden, because part of the oil is not absorbed into his body and is lost. And certainly he may not put it on a new katavolia, since part of the oil is absorbed in it and this is a use not permitted with terumah (Riko).
slab. A surface, a board.
even produce. And not only terumah bread.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTum'ot 8:8.
and one does not anoint with terumah oil with unclean hands. With impure hands, because they make the oil impure; rather he must wash his hands beforehand.

if it fell on his flesh, he may rub it with unclean hands. It is permitted to rub it without washing the hands, since the oil no longer has the status of terumah (Arukh HaShulchan 61:22, and see below, halacha 8).
within seven days. In the first seven days of his life.
he is not considered uncircumcised. Since he is obligated in circumcision only on the eighth day; for if he were uncircumcised he would be forbidden terumah (above 7:10).
and he brings his daughter's Israelite son, etc.. Since it is already profaned from its holiness after it was used (Babylonian Talmud, Keritot 7a).
and he brings his daughter's Israelite son. Not necessarily; another person too is permitted to benefit from the oil now since it is profaned (Radbaz, Riko).
and rolls it over him. He rolls it from side to side over his body, and his body too is anointed.
a non-kohen is permitted to rub him in the bathhouse. To rub the kohen's body with oil and massage him.
an Israelite woman is not permitted to rub herself after her. Since the fenugreek remains in its form and is not like oil that has been absorbed (Arukh HaShulchan 81:21).
but she may rub her hair against her hair. The Israelite woman rubs her hair against the kohenet's hair so that the fenugreek water reaches her hair.

because it is not fit as human food. And therefore it is permitted to use it ab initio in a way that destroys it (for the reason it is obligated in terumah although it is not human food, see above 2:8).
fig stems, etc.. The end of the fruit where it is attached to the tree.
the kelisin. See above 3:3.
and the insides of a watermelon. Seeds and pulp within it.
and vegetable stalk ends that householders throw away. Ends that are cut from the vegetable before cooking.

these are forbidden to non-kohanim. Because of their attachment to the fruit there is a little food in them (Melechet Shlomo, Terumot 11:4), or because when he separates them part of the fruit will be pulled off (Mishnah Rishonah there).
but vegetable stalk ends that gardeners trim are permitted to non-kohanim. Since they cut off the rotten part.
peels of beans and sesame, etc.. And likewise regarding the sanctity of the Sabbatical year (see Hilchot Shemittah 5:21 and Piskei VeShitot there).
even if the kohen did not gather them. But threw them away.
these are forbidden to non-kohanim. Since moisture remains on them that is fit for sucking.
and the other pits... and if he threw them away they are permitted. In the case of the pits of other fruits, whether the moisture is considered food depends on his intention.
the fine chaff. The delicate refuse of grain kernels.
as long as people are accustomed to beat among the threshing floors. As long as they are engaged in beating the grain on the threshing floors to separate the kernels.
the spoiled and the rotten. Moist or dry rot of fruits (Yad Peshutah).
and if they produced mold. Mildew, in which case they can no longer be eaten at all.
lees. Wine dregs.
on which he put water. In order to extract the wine that remained in them.
the first and the second are forbidden to non-kohanim. If he extracted and then extracted again, the waters are forbidden because of the wine mixed in them.
and the third is permitted. The third extraction is permitted since the wine mixed with the water is diluted.
if he added no water but strained the wine off the dregs. If he does not extract the wine with water but places the dregs in a strainer so that the wine drips out of them.
even the third is forbidden to non-priests. Since it is entirely wine.
a granary. A grain storehouse, a store.
a broom. A sweeper.
and wipes up. Gathers, absorbs.
the one who pours. The one who pours out.
the stream. The continuous flow.
it suffices. And the remnants are not taken into account.
if he put in only etc.. If he left the empty jug tilted on its side and the remnants of oil gathered, they have the law of terumah.
oil designated for burning. Oil of impure terumah.
and if he was a partner with him. And he uses the lamp for the partnership's needs.
he is not obligated to extinguish the lamp. Since it was lit permissibly.

and an Israelite may dip the wick in the priest's lamp and light it to walk by it. For this is something about which people are not particular at all (Ma'aseh Rokeach; see also Radbaz and Mishneh la-Melech, who explained it in other ways).
and a priest's garment that was woven alongside an Israelite's garment. The priest's clothing that is woven in the same place where Israelites' clothing is woven.
he may light them without the priest's permission. He does not need to ask the priest for explicit permission, since the priest too benefits from the lighting.

and likewise oil designated for burning may be lit in synagogues... without a priest's permission. Because this involves a mitzvah and a public need. Some explain that the permission is because the priest too benefits from it (see Radbaz and Riko).
and in the alleys. Lanes.

and one who has no unconsecrated oil with which to light the Chanukah lamp may light oil designated for burning without a priest's permission. Because this publicizes the miracle (Radbaz). Some explain it is because one is forbidden to benefit from this oil anyway (Derech Emunah).
oil designated for burning may be lit for the sick. For a sick person, since this is a mitzvah need (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 11:10).
with the priest's permission. Only with the priest's permission, since this involves neither a public need nor a benefit to the priest.
accustomed. Used to it.
she may light with her permission. From oil designated for burning, since she benefits from it.

for there is mixing there. Even though in these places there are many attendants who are busy with the crowd gathered there, and there is reason to fear that they may err and come to make forbidden use of the oil designated for burning (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 11:10).
they may take what they need. They may take for their needs.

one who sows terumah etc.. The Sages decreed that if one sowed terumah produce and it grew, the crops of the terumah are treated as terumah for certain purposes, even though by strict law they are entirely unconsecrated produce (see the next halakhah).
if unintentionally, it is overturned. If he sowed unintentionally, he may turn over the soil and uproot the plant (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 9:1).

and if intentionally, it is left standing. And he may not turn over the soil and spoil the plant (ibid.), since it is forbidden to destroy terumah produce, and when he sows intentionally they were strict to regard it as terumah in this respect.

and if it brought forth a third, whether intentionally or unintentionally, it is left standing. Since it has already visibly grown, even if he sowed unintentionally it already has the law of terumah crops and may not be uprooted.
and if it was flax, even if it brought forth a third and even if intentionally, it is overturned. With flax they were stricter, and in every case he must turn over the soil in order to uproot it.

they penalized him so that he would not sow with the intention of benefiting from its stalks. They penalized him so that he would not get used to sowing terumah flax seed in order to benefit from its stalks, which are the main part of the plant (Derech Emunah).
they are like unconsecrated produce in every respect. For examples of the implications see below, halakhah 27, and Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ot 11:15.
the Sages decreed upon them... on account of impure terumah etc.. And they decreed even on the crops of pure terumah.
impure terumah in the priest's hand. Which is forbidden to eat.
and he would end up stumbling through it. Lest they eat from it before sowing.
the crops of crops. The crops of the terumah that were sown and produced new crops.
unconsecrated in every respect. For something whose seed is consumed (Radbaz).

and even something whose seed is not consumed etc.. If one sowed terumah from a plant whose seed does not decay in the soil but remains whole, and from it the leaves emerge and the new plant grows, such as onions and garlic, then the seed and the first cycle of produce that grew from it are terumah crops and are forbidden. But if these were gathered and sown a second time, and the second cycle of produce is greater than what was sown, it nullifies the prohibition in the original. And although this is a plant whose seed is not consumed, whose crops generally do not neutralize the prohibition in the original (see Hilchot Kilayim 5:24), here the crops of crops are permitted, because it is a prohibition originating in a rabbinic decree of distancing (see Yad Peshutah).
and likewise terumah outside the Land. Above 1:6.
and the mixture of terumah. Terumah that became mixed with unconsecrated produce, where the unconsecrated produce is not enough to nullify the terumah.
and the additional terumah. Terumah that must be added where he initially separated less than the amount fixed by the Sages (above 3:6).
that are not eaten. That are not customarily eaten.
such as turnip seed and radish seed. That were taken from terumah turnips and radishes, sown, and produced crops.
and likewise one who sows flax etc.. For its seed too is included among inedible garden seeds (Riko and Kesef Mishneh).
even though the crops are pure. For after the seed takes root, what grows from it is pure (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 2:19).

saplings of unconsecrated produce that became impure etc.. If he planted impure unconsecrated produce intending to separate terumah from the pure crops that would grow, the terumah is permitted for priests to eat as pure terumah, since there was never a stage at which it was impure terumah.

an ear of grain that was within the heap etc.. This halakhah speaks of an ear whose chaff he had not removed and which was not yet obligated in terumot and ma'aserot, that was within a pile of grain at the time their work was completed and they became obligated in terumot and ma'aserot, and so it too became obligated along with them.

and smoothed the heap. He threshed the pile, smoothed it and cleaned the straw from it, and thereby its work was completed and it became obligated in terumot and ma'aserot (see Hilchot Ma'aser 2:1, 3:1).
he planted it. While it was still untithed produce.
and afterward designated it and made it terumah. For the heap in which it was smoothed.
and it becomes like produce whose work has not yet been completed. Like produce whose work was not completed and that was sown, from which terumah cannot be made (Derech Emunah).
if he plucked from it. After he had made it terumah.
if intentionally, he is liable to death etc.. As for one who eats terumah (above 10:1).
he bent down. He stooped.
his intention is nullified in the view of all people etc.. And one is liable for eating terumah only for something that is normally eaten (see above 10:2).
and the added fifth. But he pays the principal like a robber, if the priest had already acquired the terumah.
a field of terumah crops is subject to gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner etc.. For by strict law the produce is entirely unconsecrated.
and poor Israelites may sell etc.. Since terumah crops are forbidden to non-priests, the solution for an Israelite or Levite who has such produce is to sell it to a priest.
for the price of terumah. Terumah is sold more cheaply than unconsecrated produce because it is permitted only to priests.
one who beats these crops. With sticks, to separate the kernels from the straw, and not in the usual way, by threshing with animals.
commendable. Since in this way there is no concern that the animal will eat of them.
he hangs baskets etc.. He hangs a basket of the same kind of produce on the animal's neck so that it will eat from that and not from the terumah crops.

he thus neither muzzles the animal nor feeds it terumah. In this way he avoids the prohibition of muzzling the animal while it threshes (see Hilchot Sekhirut 13:2), and also of feeding it something he may not feed it.
like other consecrated things. See Hilchot Pesulei ha-Mukdashin 18:12.
and he may not bring it to impurity. He may not cause it to be able to become impure.

and it is permitted to defile terumah of outside the Land with Torah-level impurities etc.. The Sages decreed impurity on people and vessels outside the Land, out of concern that they were defiled by corpse impurity (Hilchot Tum'at Met 11:1). Although terumah of outside the Land is impure on this account by rabbinic law alone, it is permitted to defile it even with Torah-level impurity, because its entire obligation is rabbinic.

a menstruant may separate challah outside the Land. A menstruant, whose impurity is Torah-level, may separate challah from her dough even though she defiles it (and challah is called terumah, Hilchot Bikkurim 5:13), since the obligation to separate challah outside the Land is rabbinic (see ibid. 5:5).
for it is only forbidden to eat it... as we have explained. Above 7:8 (and see also Hilchot Bikkurim 5:10-12).
and it is to be burned. As with impure terumah, above 11:1.
and there are cases of doubt in which terumah is burned. There are cases in which terumah is burned even when it is only possibly impure.
as will be explained in the matter of impurity and purity. See Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ot 13:13.
he may not move it from its place. To a place where it would be better guarded, or alternatively to a place where it would easily be lost (based on Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 8:8).
and he may not uncover it. In a way that would make it forbidden to eat because of the danger of uncovered liquids (Tiferet Yisrael there; and see below halakhah 13).
and we are not concerned that it may be eaten. During the time he keeps it until it becomes impure.
a jug. Of terumah wine.
in the upper winepress. The place where grapes are trodden, from which the wine flows to the lower winepress, which is the collecting pit for the must.

if he can save a revi'it of it in purity, he should save it. And he may not touch the wine with hands that are not pure, or collect it in impure vessels, in order to save the unconsecrated wine in the pit from loss.

he may save it with his hands without washing them etc.. It is permitted to prevent the terumah wine from reaching the lower winepress even if he thereby defiles it, since the wine was going to become impure anyway because of the winepress, and they permitted defiling it with the hands in order to save the rest of the wine from loss (Radbaz; and see the next halakhah).
even though he defiles it, as will be explained in the matter of purities. For the Sages decreed impurity on anyone who touches terumah without washing the hands (Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ot 8:8).
when does this apply. That they permitted him to save it without washing his hands when he cannot save a revi'it in purity.
for it would all become terumah-mixed and be lost. For the impure terumah wine would not be nullified in the unconsecrated wine, and the entire mixture would be of no use.

for it is nullified at one to a hundred. Terumah is nullified when there are a hundred parts of unconsecrated produce against it (below 13:1), and all the wine in the mixture has the law of impure unconsecrated wine, which may be drunk.

or if a jug of oil were to fall and become impure. With terumah oil they were strict not to save it with the hands, even if the unconsecrated oil is not a hundred times as much and the entire mixture will be classed as impure terumah oil, since impure terumah oil has a use for lighting.
and likewise a jug of oil that was spilled. On its own, and if he does not save it, it will be lost.

because he is in a hurry. The Sages were lenient in certain cases where a person is hurried about his property (see Hilchot Shabbat 6:22; and the Or Sameach explained that the situation is urgent: if he does not save it in impurity, everything will spill, and so they permitted it so that the terumah could be used for lighting).
and loaves of terumah. Loaves of bread made from terumah grain.
