so that he not defile the terumah with his hands. For if he gives it by hand to a gentile, it becomes impure the moment the gentile touches it (since the Sages decreed impurity on gentiles; see Hilchot Metamei Mishkav u-Moshav 2:10), and he would thus have defiled the terumah directly.

fenugreek and vetches of terumah, since they are not human food. But rather animal food. Nevertheless they are subject to terumot and ma'aserot, since many people eat them in various situations: fenugreek while it is still a vegetable (above 2:8), and vetches in times of distress and famine (above 2:2).

he is careful only at the time of soaking them in water etc.. He must be careful that the soaking in water be done in purity, since the water first makes them susceptible to impurity, and when he soaks them and touches them with his hands he makes them susceptible and defiles them at once; this is what the Sages were particular about even for fenugreek and vetches (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Ma'aser Sheni 2:3).

therefore terumah of fenugreek and vetches may be given to a priest who is an am ha-aretz. For the reason terumah is not given to an am ha-aretz priest is so that he not defile it (above 6:2), and in this case there is no such concern.
terumah is not deposited with an am ha-aretz priest because he is overly familiar with it. There is concern that he will not be careful about defiling it, since he is accustomed to eating it.
in an earthenware vessel sealed with a tight-fitting lid. A vessel with a tightly fastened cover that protects what is inside from receiving impurity (see Hilchot Tum'at Met 6:3).
provided the produce is not susceptible to impurity. Produce that has been rendered susceptible to impurity by liquids.

a decree lest his wife, a menstruant, move them. For a menstruant defiles even by moving something without direct contact, and even if it is sealed with a tight-fitting lid (Hilchot Metamei Mishkav u-Moshav 8:2-3).

one does not do for an am ha-aretz etc.. A person who is careful about impurity and purity and works at an olive press (a badad) should not separate terumah in purity for an am ha-aretz, lest the latter defile it. But if the am ha-aretz wants to pay him for the whole process of extracting oil from the olives, they permitted him to do so because it is his livelihood ('his sustenance'), and he should do everything he can to keep the terumah from becoming impure, by placing it in a vessel that cannot become impure and warning the am ha-aretz to touch only the vessel and not the terumah (see also Hilchot Bikkurim 8:12).

be careful lest you touch the terumah, or it will not return to being untithed produce. Although the terumah does not revert to untithed produce because of his touch, they threaten him with this so that he will not touch and defile the terumah (Radbaz, Hilchot Bikkurim there). Some explain that the terumah does indeed revert to untithed produce (since the Sages instituted that the badad's separation of terumah is conditional on the am ha-aretz not defiling it; Chatam Sofer, Gittin 62a).
an Israelite who processes his produce in impurity. Who handles his produce in a way that defiles it.
one does not harvest grapes with him. Since he will afterward defile the grapes from which terumah will be separated, and one may not strengthen the hands of transgressors.
and needless to say one does not tread with him. To produce wine, which would then become impure.

but one may carry jugs with him to the winepress and bring them from the winepress. After he has already defiled the wine and the transgression has been done, this is not strengthening the hands of transgressors (Commentary on the Mishnah, Avodah Zarah 4:9; and see Hilchot Bikkurim 8:13).
he squeezes them and makes them terumah. And the terumah is pure, if he did so in the manner explained below.

and squeezed them in amounts each less than an egg's bulk, the liquid that comes out of them is permitted etc.. In squeezing, the fruit touches the liquid and can defile it, but impure food defiles only if it amounts to the size of an egg (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 4:1); therefore liquid extracted from impure fruit in amounts less than an egg's bulk is not defiled by it.
for libations. Wine placed on the altar.
for the liquid is as if it were deposited within the food. And it does not become impure when the food becomes impure.

they said 'less than an egg's bulk' only as a decree, lest he squeeze more than an egg's bulk and the liquid be defiled by an egg's bulk. By strict law it would have been possible to permit squeezing even fruit of exactly an egg's bulk, since the liquid that comes out reduces the grapes below the size of an egg and they can no longer defile it; but the Sages decreed that one squeeze only less than an egg's bulk each time, for if they permitted squeezing an egg's bulk, there is concern that he might squeeze more than an egg's bulk, and the liquid that came out first would be defiled by the fruit.

and if this fruit was third-degree impure. The condition of squeezing less than an egg's bulk was stated only for fruit that is second-degree impure, that is, that touched something first-degree impure, since with terumah, what touches a second-degree becomes impure and is made third-degree, but a third-degree does not defile other food.
he may tread them in the winepress or the olive press. And there is no need to tread in amounts less than an egg's bulk.

for a third-degree impure item does not make a fourth-degree in terumah. Terumah that is third-degree impure does not defile other terumah to make it fourth-degree, and therefore the terumah fruit do not defile the liquid that comes out of them.
as will be explained in the matter of purities. See Hilchot She'ar Avot ha-Tum'ot 11:3.
among the wood. Intended for burning.
and afterward he heats an oven and a stove with them. As with impure terumah.
they bury them. So that no one comes to stumble through them.
that was left uncovered. Left exposed, without covering or supervision.

since it is forbidden to drink. Because of the danger that a venomous snake or the like drank from it and left venom in it (for details of the laws of uncovered liquids see Hilchot Rotze'ach 11:5-16).
because of danger to life. Lest they have been eaten by an animal that left venom there (ibid. 12:2).
it is to be burned. Because of the water mixed into it (see also ibid. 11:16).
for they belong to the owners to give to whichever priest they wish. The right to choose to whom to give the terumah remains with the owner.
and each man's holy things shall be his. The owners have a certain ownership over their consecrated gifts, and terumah is included among consecrated things.
and the benefit of giving. The benefit one can receive for giving the terumah to a particular priest.
is not money. It is not considered actual money that can be claimed in court (see also Hilchot Genevah 2:5 and Hilchot Ishut 5:6).
lest others placed them there until they could take them. And before they managed to take them, the owners gave the produce to a priest together with what had been hidden in it.
Israelites are not obligated to attend to the terumah and bring it etc.. For this is not part of the obligation of giving.
and he may take payment for bringing it from the priest. From the priest to whom he gives the terumah, since he is not obligated by strict law to attend to it.
this is a desecration of God's name. Because terumah is holy and must be treated with honor.
to assist at the threshing floors in order to receive their gifts. To help with the work of the threshing floor so that the owner of the crop will give them the terumot and the tithe.
he has fulfilled the obligation of giving. Since a gift given on condition that it be returned is considered a gift (see, for example, Hilchot Bikkurim 11:8).
because he appears to be assisting at the threshing floors. For the priest helps the owner of the produce be rid of the obligation of giving, and thereby assists him.
the Omnipresent. The Holy One, blessed be He.
to the guard of his winepress. The priest.
firstborn. A firstborn animal, which is given to the priest (Hilchot Bekhorot 1:1-2).
gifts. The foreleg, jaws and maw given to the priest from the slaughter of a pure animal (Hilchot Bikkurim 9:1).
unless he first gave them payment for their guarding. In that case the giving is not part of the payment.

when does this apply etc.. Only when the owners intended to give the gift for free to one of two priests or Levites is it permitted to accept payment from another person in order to give to one of them.
for the benefit of giving. In exchange for some consideration.
this is forbidden. Since it looks like a sale, which is forbidden with terumot, as detailed shortly.
even though etc.. Even though he is not selling his own terumah to a priest, but buying terumah belonging to a priest and selling it to another priest.
or they feed it. To their household members, such as an uncircumcised or impure priest, who are forbidden terumah but whose household members are permitted it by virtue of him (above 7:12).

and a minor who has the sense to spread out his lap. Who knows to spread the corners of his garment to serve as a container for the produce. Although in practice he is able to receive terumah and guard it, they do not distribute to him at the threshing floors.
because these lack understanding... because they are a separate category. Because it shows disrespect to consecrated things to give them to such people openly (Meiri, Yevamot 99b).
and a slave... and they testify about him that he is a priest. See Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 20:11.
and a woman. A priest's wife, who eats by virtue of her husband.
lest she be divorced. And they would not know it, and she would take it on the presumption that she is a priest's wife.

and because of seclusion. Even if it is known that she is still married to the priest, one should not give to a woman, out of concern for the prohibition of seclusion, since threshing floors are located outside the city.
and one who marries a woman who is unfit for him. For example a priest who married a divorced woman.
and all of them are sent to their homes. Terumah, in which case these concerns do not arise.

and they distribute to them of the other holy things of the border and send them to their homes. They give them consecrated things that are given to the priest outside the Temple, such as challah, and send them to their homes as with terumah.
except for one who marries a woman unfit for him. As a penalty.

and the impure and the uncircumcised. Who are not fit to eat terumah. Although they are fit to feed their household members, it is not sent to them since they are not fit to eat it themselves (Derech Emunah).
it rises. It is nullified and becomes permitted.
he separates one se'ah from all of it and gives it to the priest. Since the mixture contains a se'ah of terumah belonging to the priest.
such as the terumah of the kelisin etc.. See above 3:3, and see also Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 15:15.

the whole becomes a terumah mixture. The entire mixture has the law of terumah regarding the law of eating it and the guarding of its purity. The term 'mixture of terumah' (medumma) derives from the fact that terumah is also called 'dema' in the Torah (Exodus 22:28; Commentary on the Mishnah, Demai 1:3).

and everything is sold to priests at the price of terumah, except for the price of that se'ah. For the mixture belongs mainly to the owner, but is to be treated as terumah; therefore he sells it to priests apart from the price of the se'ah that already belonged to the priests before it was mixed. He sells them the produce at a lower value than unconsecrated produce (the 'price of terumah') since it may be eaten only by priests and must be eaten in purity.
when a kind was mixed with its own kind. And the taste of the terumah cannot be identified.

but when a kind was mixed with a different kind, it is by imparting taste. Nullification does not depend on quantities but on whether the terumah imparted taste to the mixture (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 15:1-6 and the commentary there).

everything is permitted to non-priests. Since the terumah is nullified, and he also need not set aside the se'ah that fell, since its taste is nullified and, in addition, something like what fell cannot be separated, because it was mixed with a different kind (Aruch HaShulchan 86:4).
and he lifted out a se'ah from all of it. In order to give it to the priest, as above in halakhah 1.

it renders terumah-mixture only in proportion. Although he lifted it out to give to the priest, it does not have the status of terumah since it is mixed with unconsecrated produce; only the proportional share of terumah in it is considered. Therefore it suffices that the unconsecrated produce into which it falls be a hundred times that proportional share of terumah in the se'ah (though the unconsecrated part of the se'ah itself does not combine, even if it contains a hundred to nullify it; Aruch HaShulchan 86:11).
and the whole becomes terumah-mixed. For a tenth of the mixture is terumah, and from each se'ah he takes out of the mixture, a tenth is terumah.
less than ten se'ah. From the first mixture.
they do not render terumah-mixture. If, by calculation, the unconsecrated produce into which they fell is more than a hundred times the terumah.
to be mixed. To be thoroughly mixed.

and if the majority is unconsecrated, it is like unconsecrated produce and does not render terumah-mixture, even though all of it is forbidden to non-priests. Although the first mixture is forbidden to non-priests because it lacks a hundred against the terumah, nevertheless if the majority of it is unconsecrated and some of it fell elsewhere, it does not forbid the produce into which it fell.
he lifted it out. He lifted a se'ah out of the mixture to give it to the priest.

the unconsecrated produce is permitted until the terumah exceeds the unconsecrated produce. For by strict law a kind in its own kind is nullified by a majority, and the Sages required nullification at a hundred. Here, since the se'ahs of terumah did not fall all at once, the Sages were lenient, so that each se'ah that falls separately is nullified and they do not combine to forbid the unconsecrated produce.
if he knew of the first one. He knew that it fell.
they are not mixed. The knowledge separates the falls, and each se'ah that fell is nullified even though he did not lift out a se'ah between the falls to give to the priest.
and it should have risen. Since there was a way to nullify it, it is treated as if it were nullified.

the refuse of terumah does not combine... but refuse etc.. Refuse combines with the food to be lenient and not to be strict: on one hand it is not considered food and so does not require nullification, and on the other it is considered part of the quantity of the unconsecrated produce and can help nullify the terumah.
good wheat. That has little refuse relative to the flour.
for the bran. The coarse refuse of the grain.
for the unconsecrated produce increased and the terumah decreased. The unconsecrated produce increased proportionally because of the abundance of refuse mixed in with it.
to a hundred logs of cloudy wine. Which has dregs mixed in.

the dregs in it are not removed; rather the log rises. The dregs are not subtracted from the amount of unconsecrated wine but are counted with it, and if there are a hundred logs of unconsecrated cloudy wine against the clear log, it is nullified in them.

and likewise if a cloudy log fell into a hundred clear logs, the dregs in it are not removed. The dregs are not subtracted from the quantity of terumah, and a hundred logs of unconsecrated wine are needed to nullify it, since they are not classed as the refuse of terumah that does not combine (as above, halakhah 7), because it is customary to drink them with the wine and they were formed from the body of the wine itself (Radbaz).

for water does not make the wine rise. It does not combine to count as wine and nullify the log as if it were a hundred of wine. See the Raavad's critique, who wrote that water does nullify wine by imparting taste, but here the wine and water do not combine to nullify because their measures for nullification are not equal (wine in wine is nullified at a hundred because it is a kind in its own kind, whereas water nullifies wine when the wine does not impart taste to it, so water does not combine to make up a hundred). The commentators wrote that Maimonides too agrees with this (see below 15:17).
until they exceeded a hundred. So that the mixture contains more than a hundred parts of unconsecrated produce relative to the amount of terumah.

the whole is terumah-mixed, for one may not nullify Torah prohibitions in advance. And the Sages penalized, so that if he transgressed and nullified it, it is not nullified (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 15:25).
terumah of outside the Land. The obligation to separate which is rabbinic (above 1:6).

it is permitted to nullify it by a majority. With terumah of outside the Land they were lenient to permit nullifying it in advance, and moreover they were lenient that it is nullified by a majority and nullification at a hundred is not required.
and he eats it during the days of his impurity. Since the terumah is nullified, the priest may eat it while impure.

and moreover, if he had wine etc.. The Sages were further lenient, so that one may add to two logs of unconsecrated wine two logs of terumah one after the other, and likewise add another log of terumah after removing one log from the mixture, even though now the majority will be terumah. Nullification in this manner is based on the principle that each log of terumah that falls is nullified by the majority and does not combine with what fell earlier ('each earlier one is nullified'). Nevertheless they did not permit mixing three separate logs one after the other without removing a log in between, so as not to create a clear majority of terumah (Riko).
one who sows terumah beside unconsecrated produce. And what grows from the terumah is 'terumah crops', which the Sages penalized by forbidding them to non-priests (above 11:21).
in a garden bed. A plot of sown ground (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 5:9).
with something whose seed is consumed in the ground. For example grain, where the terumah seed itself rots in the soil and a completely new plant grows in its place.
but something whose seed does not perish in the ground. For example onions and the like, where the terumah onion remains in the ground and puts out leaves each year.
the whole is terumah-mixed. For when its seed is not consumed, each plant is considered to stand on its own and there is no mixture here (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
and he may not pluck in advance. For one does not nullify a prohibition in advance (above, halakhah 10).
baskets. Baskets.
the crops are unconsecrated in every respect. For they were lenient in a case of doubtful terumah crops.
and the second he treats as terumah. Out of doubt.
to another place. Where there is unconsecrated produce.

it does not render terumah-mixture. For each of them is possibly terumah, and since they fell into different places, each mixture stands on its own and is permitted out of doubt, as perhaps the terumah fell into the other.
both fell into one place. In which case terumah certainly became mixed in that place, and the only doubt is which basket the terumah was in.
they render terumah-mixture like the smaller of the two. A hundred times the amount in the smaller basket is required.
the crops are unconsecrated. As with a mixture of terumah crops and unconsecrated crops.
and with something whose seed is not consumed, the crops are terumah-mixed. For the crops are not considered mixed, and each crop is possibly terumah crops and possibly unconsecrated crops.
the crops are unconsecrated. For each crop stands on its own.

for attached and detached are not made proof for one another. Since one is detached and one is attached, they are not treated as a mixture of unconsecrated and terumah crops, but each crop is a separate doubt whether it is unconsecrated crops or terumah crops, and it is permitted.
for I say etc.. The Sages were lenient in this case to attribute it and rely on the possibility that the unconsecrated produce fell among unconsecrated produce and the terumah among terumah.
even though the unconsecrated produce did not exceed the terumah. This permission applies even where one cannot rely on nullification by a majority.
until the unconsecrated produce exceeds the terumah. For by Torah law terumah is nullified by a majority.
a se'ah of terumah. That he separated from one heap.
that fell into the heap. Another heap of untithed produce that is subject to terumah.
and said, 'the terumah of this heap is within it'. He designated the terumah but did not define its location.

in the place where that se'ah fell, there the terumah of the heap is fixed. Since he did not specify the place of separation of the terumah, we assume he intended it to be next to the terumah that had already fallen into the heap (Aruch HaShulchan 87:29-30).

and everything becomes mixed with the terumah that fell and with the terumah of the heap. And a hundred times the amount of unconsecrated produce is needed in the pile against both, in order to nullify them.
he said, 'the terumah of the heap is in its north'. If he specified that the terumah is in the north of the pile, but did not set it apart from the rest of the pile.

he divides it in two etc.. Some explained that this means dividing the heap into four quarters, and the northern quarter is what is called here 'the north of its north' (Mirkevet ha-Mishneh, and so it seems from the Tosefta 4:9, where it says 'he makes it like an X', meaning the Greek letter chi). Others explained that one divides the northern half into a northern and a southern part, and the northern end is 'the north of its north' (Minchat Bikkurim on the Tosefta there; see also the gloss of the Vilna Gaon).
that is the terumah mixture. Of the terumah he separated, and the rest of the pile is unconsecrated.
heaps. Piles.
in one of them. And he did not specify in which.
both are terumah-mixed. And each is to be treated as terumah-mixed because of the two terumot.
and it is not known which it is. The heap is permitted, and each se'ah is possibly terumah and possibly untithed produce.
and it is not known which is the one tithed from the untithed produce. And each of them is possibly unconsecrated and possibly untithed.
fifty black figs and fifty white. In one place.
and the white ones are terumah-mixed. Since there are not a hundred of them to nullify the terumah, and all of them must be treated as terumah.
it rises at one to a hundred from all of it. All hundred figs combine to nullify it.

they are all terumah-mixed. Since he knew which one fell, it immediately renders terumah-mixed those like it, and he has before him two groups of figs of which one is terumah-mixed. The forgetting afterward does not change this situation, and both are forbidden because of the doubt.
and likewise rounds of pressed figs and rectangles of pressed figs. Figs that were pressed together into a round or rectangular shape.

they nullify, whether by count or by weight etc.. The Sages were lenient in this case, so that one may assume that a small round fell, and whether there are a hundred rounds against it or a hundred times its weight in them, even if there are not a hundred rounds, the round is nullified.
I say a small one fell, and he lifts out one small one. And he need not give the priest a large round, since it is not known which fell, and one does not take money from a person out of doubt.

a round fell into forty rounds... I say a small one fell etc.. Even though there are only forty rounds in the mixture, the rounds nullify the terumah round because there are a hundred times its weight.
ritlin. A unit of weight, the same as the litra mentioned shortly (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 4:10).

and flour and fine flour do not combine. Although both are made of wheat, they are not considered one thing, but like black and white figs, with regard to nullifying terumah (see Aruch HaShulchan 88:8).
the granary. A grain storehouse, a store.
together with a little of the unconsecrated produce that it fell upon. To make sure he took all the terumah.
like one who gathers wheat from on top of barley. Who gathers a little barley along with the wheat.
granaries. A plural form of 'megurah' (some read 'megurot', and the two forms are interchangeable).
because it is easy to gather the two into one house. People are accustomed to carrying and mixing them, since they are small.
and how does he nullify a se'ah that fell. In a case where the baskets or granaries combine to nullify it and a se'ah must be given to the priest.
from one of the two. The entire quantity that fell.
like the law of jars full of unconsecrated figs on which he pressed etc.. That he pressed terumah figs onto the mouth of one of the jars and does not know which.
and he sells it to a priest except for the price of that litra. And thus he nullifies the terumah that fell.
the openings are all terumah-mixed. The figs at the mouths of all the jars are to be treated as terumah.
and the bottoms. What is at the bottom of the jars.
on the mouth of a basket or on the mouth of a round. And he also pressed unconsecrated figs onto the mouths of baskets and other rounds.
round. A vessel in which figs are packed to form a round mass of figs.
and it is not known which one it is. It is not known where exactly he pressed it.
he pressed it. The litra of terumah.
on the mouth of a round. And there are several rounds there, and now one of them is terumah-mixed.

we regard them as if they were separate. Since it is not known where exactly the litra is at the mouths of the rounds, we do not consider only the figs at the openings (as in the previous halakhah), but all the figs are measured for nullification (see Kesef Mishneh and Mirkevet ha-Mishneh).

for a doubt of terumah is nullified by a majority of unconsecrated produce. In each round there is a doubt whether the terumah is in it, and so it needs a majority of unconsecrated produce within itself.
its certain case. When it is known that there is terumah in the mixture.
and its doubtful case. When there is doubt whether it remains in the mixture, as explained below.
and it has no permission except by a majority. That it exceed the mixture and be nullified at a hundred, which is the majority required to nullify terumah (as explained in the next halakhah).
and if it was in more than fifty, it does not need a majority. As explained in the next halakhah.
as we have explained. Above 13:2.

one fell into fifty and one of the whole was lost. This is the second case mentioned in the previous halakhah ('its doubtful case forbids at fifty'), in which a terumah fig fell into fifty unconsecrated figs and one fig was lost from this mixture.
these are forbidden. Perhaps the terumah fig is among the fifty that remain.

and he adds to them fifty figs and one. So that the mixture has a hundred and one figs. Although one may not nullify a prohibition (above 13:10), here they permitted it because it is doubtful whether there is terumah here.
and if one of terumah fell into fifty-one. Here the third case is detailed, 'and if it was in more than fifty'.

the rest are permitted to non-priests. For a doubt of terumah is nullified in fifty-one, as we treat the mixture as if it contains one fig that is possibly terumah; and just as certain terumah is nullified at a hundred and one, so doubtful terumah is nullified at half that. Therefore it suffices for fifty-one figs to remain in the mixture to nullify it (Aruch HaShulchan 88:22).
whose terumah had not been taken. The terumah of the tithe, which the Levite must give to the priest from the tithe.

he designates the terumah of the tithe etc.. He separates the terumah of the tithe by speech, but does not separate it physically, lest he take from the great terumah. Now the produce is unconsecrated but has terumah and terumah of the tithe mixed into it, and therefore he sells all of it to priests and they pay him only for the unconsecrated part of the mixture.
these are redeemed. And the produce becomes unconsecrated except for the terumah that fell.
a se'ah of impure terumah that fell into less than a hundred etc.. And since it was not nullified at a hundred, the entire mixture is forbidden to eat, with the law of impure terumah.
until they rot. And then he may throw them away.
rather he lights it all. He burns them immediately and does not leave them until they rot.
in the way that impure terumah is burned. Above 12:12.

that fell into less than a hundred of impure unconsecrated produce. And the terumah does not become impure from being mixed, since food becomes impure only if it was moistened with water or one of the liquids that make food susceptible to impurity (see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:1-2).

and the priest eats this terumah-mixture parched. The impure unconsecrated produce is permitted to eat, and so is the pure terumah, but care must be taken that the terumah be eaten without becoming impure; therefore he parches the mixture or bakes it without liquid, and eats it that way.
with fruit juices that do not make susceptible. To receive impurity.

or he may knead this terumah-mixture in amounts each less than an egg's bulk. If he wants to knead it with water, he can take less than an egg's bulk of the mixture each time and knead it by itself, or mix it into another pure dough; in these cases the portion of impure unconsecrated produce in the mixture is less than an egg's bulk and cannot defile the terumah.
for impure food does not defile etc.. See above 12:11.

and it is eaten parched etc.. As for the se'ah that was lifted out as terumah, it is to be treated as if it were a mixture of pure and impure produce that are permitted to eat, and it is to be eaten in a way that the pure does not become impure from the impure, as explained above in halakhah 12.

for the se'ah that fell etc.. For if we regarded the se'ah that was lifted as the se'ah that fell, the law would be that impure terumah that fell into pure produce is lifted and burned, and pure terumah that fell into impure produce is lifted and eaten as usual.
it rises at one to a hundred. For the terumah was nullified in the mixture, and the prohibition of a terumah mixture does not apply to it.
and everything is eaten as pure terumah. The whole mixture is treated as pure terumah.
and if it fell into less than a hundred, he leaves everything until it rots. Since it was not nullified, the entire mixture is treated as impure terumah.
two baskets. Of unconsecrated produce, with not a hundred in them to nullify the terumah.
and afterward a second se'ah fell. Of terumah.

we say it fell in the same place the first fell etc.. The later authorities wrote that this permission to attribute the matter to the one already spoiled applies only to rabbinic terumah, as above 13:14 (Aruch HaShulchan 89:14, Derech Emunah, Yad Peshutah).

we do not say that the second fell where the first fell, nor that the first fell where the second fell. Since both were already spoiled after the first fell, and we do not retroactively attribute that the one spoiled by the second se'ah was also spoiled by the first.
we say it fell into the impure one. For here too we attribute the spoiling to what is already spoiled.

two baskets etc.. In halakhot 17-21 the commentators of Maimonides found it hard to explain the laws as the text reads here, and some suggested (by comparison with Tosefta Terumot 5:16 and the Yerushalmi there 7:3) reversing the text here: according to this, the case at the start of halakhah 17 (pure terumah and impure unconsecrated produce) should be at the start of halakhah 20, and the case at the start of halakhah 20 (impure terumah and pure unconsecrated produce) should be at the start of halakhah 17 (Riko; see also Kesef Mishneh and Aruch HaShulchan 69:16-20, who emended in other ways). Below the explanations of the laws will be given according to the text before us, and according to the possibility of reversing the text in Maimonides.
a se'ah of pure terumah fell into one of them. And there is not a hundred to nullify it.
we say it fell into the terumah one. And we attribute it leniently, and do not change the status of the unconsecrated produce.

and the unconsecrated produce is eaten in purity like terumah. That the priest eats it with bodily purity, lest the pure terumah be there (Radbaz, Yad Peshutah based on the responsum of R. Yosef ha-Nagid no. 59). According to Riko's emendation, this speaks of baskets of impure terumah and pure unconsecrated produce, and we say the terumah fell into the basket of impure terumah and must be burned, and the unconsecrated produce is eaten in purity lest the terumah have fallen into it (and according to his emendation that the unconsecrated produce is pure, it is easier to understand why it does not say here that the unconsecrated produce should be eaten parched or kneaded with fruit juices).

18-19. and the unconsecrated produce is eaten parched or kneaded with fruit juices. Although both the unconsecrated produce and the terumah are impure, one must be strict in this, not to add impurity to the impure terumah if it fell into the unconsecrated produce (Yad Peshutah, based on R. Yosef ha-Nagid). And according to Riko's emendation that this speaks of baskets of impure terumah and pure unconsecrated produce, it is understandable why one must take care not to cause the unconsecrated produce to become susceptible to impurity, since we are concerned that the impure terumah fell into the unconsecrated produce and defiled it.

and the unconsecrated produce is eaten parched. Even though both the unconsecrated produce and the terumah are pure, one must be careful about this so as not to make the terumah susceptible to impurity (R. Yosef ha-Nagid, cited in Kesef Mishneh; and see another explanation of this reading in Riko). And according to Riko's emendation that this speaks of baskets of pure terumah and impure unconsecrated produce, it is understandable why one must take care that the pure terumah not be defiled by the impure unconsecrated produce.

a se'ah of impure terumah fell into one of them, both are forbidden, for a doubt of impure terumah is forbidden etc.. The commentators found it hard to understand why in this case we do not attribute that the terumah fell into the terumah basket, as in the previous cases. Riko, on the basis of his emendation that these are baskets of pure terumah and impure unconsecrated produce, explained that one must be uncertain whether to attribute that terumah fell into terumah or that the impurity fell into impurity, and therefore one must be strict with both baskets. One may say that we attribute that terumah fell into the terumah basket only when the terumah did not forbid what it fell into. But in a case where impure terumah fell into pure, it makes it forbidden just as it does the unconsecrated produce, and therefore one should not assume that it fell specifically into the terumah basket and not the unconsecrated produce (based on Aruch HaShulchan 69:20; and see Yad Peshutah, who strove to reconcile the text as it stands in Maimonides).
on the principles. According to the rules.
that we explained in Hilchot Issurei Ma'akhalot. Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot, chapter 15.
a sealed jug. Which was sealed after being filled with terumah.
that became mixed with several thousand sealed jugs. Of unconsecrated produce.

the whole becomes terumah-mixed. All the jugs are to be treated as terumah, and the jug is not nullified at a hundred since a sealed jug is one of seven items that are not nullified because of their importance (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 16:3-4).

and we say that it was the one of terumah that fell. One may be lenient and assume that the terumah jug is the one that fell, and there is no need to lift out one jug as terumah. Although if it had remained in the mixture it would have had no nullification, even by lifting out one jug for the priest (as explained above in halakhah 1), the Sages were lenient in the case where one of them fell into the sea.
and a fig and the like, its falling is not recognizable. Therefore they did not permit in this case, lest they come to permit even if none fell (based on Rashi, Zevachim 74b).
and it was opened. But one may not open it in advance (Riko, based on the Gemara).

he takes one out of a hundred from it and drinks the jug. Since it was opened, it left the category of a mixture of sealed jugs, and it is treated as a mixture of terumah that is nullified at a hundred, from which one out of a hundred is lifted for the priest and the rest is permitted.
he takes from them enough for their terumah-mixing, one jug. He takes one jug against the amount of terumah that got mixed and gives it to the priest.
and the other fifty are forbidden. As long as they have not been opened, their law is still that of terumah.

and we do not presume that the jug of terumah is in the majority. One cannot rely on the majority of jugs having been opened and assume that the terumah jug is among them and the other fifty are unconsecrated.
all of them are terumah-mixed. And the terumah jug has no nullification.
and the rest are terumah-mixed. The other jugs that have not yet been opened.
we have already explained in Hilchot Issurei Ma'akhalot. Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 16:1.

for one who leavens and one who seasons forbids even in the smallest amount. Food ingredients intended for leavening or seasoning, which have a very noticeable effect on the food, are not nullified even if there is only a small amount of them in the food.
even its yolk is forbidden. Although it is in the inner part of the egg.
sourdough. Sour dough intended to leaven other doughs.
and he lifted it out. He separated it from the dough.
it is permitted. Although it affected the leavening of the dough, since it was lifted out before its effect was felt.
we have already explained. Above 13:2.
by imparting taste. The law of the mixture depends on whether the taste of the terumah is noticeable in it.
lentils that were cooked etc.. In this halakhah there is no distinction whether the onion is terumah and the lentils unconsecrated, or the reverse (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 10:1).
this is permitted. And this is a special law for lentils and onions, as explained later in the halakhah.
and any other dish. A dish that is not lentils, which absorbs both when cooked and when the onion is whole.
its pitma. The protrusion from which the roots of the onion branch (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 1:2).
or if it was moist. In which case there is no good separation between it and the lentils.
and the kaplot. A leek found in the Land of Israel.
one who pickles. In salt, vinegar or something else.
this is permitted to non-priests. And we are not concerned that they imparted taste to each other.
except for kinds of onions etc.. Whose taste is sharp and which impart taste to what is pickled with them.
and chatzir. Leek-garlic, called 'karti' in the language of the Sages (based on Targum Onkelos on Numbers 11:5 and Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 17:5).
the onion is permitted to non-priests. Since it imparts taste to the vegetable and does not receive taste from it.
crushed ones. Ground up (Commentary on the Mishnah, Terumot 10:7).
or pickled them. The crushed unconsecrated produce.
in terumah liquid. Water in which terumah produce was soaked or in which a liquid from terumah produce is mixed (ibid.).
because the crushed ones absorb from the whole ones. And not the reverse.
absorb. Absorb taste.
water of pickling and water of boiling of terumah. Water in which terumah was pickled or boiled.
these are forbidden to non-priests. Since they have absorbed the taste of terumah.
dill. Shamir, a seasoning plant.
it has the law of terumah. It is to be treated as terumah.

but once it has imparted taste to the pot, it has no law of terumah. Since it is intended only to impart taste, what remains of it after imparting taste is like refuse, as it is not fit to eat (Commentary on the Mishnah, Uktzin 3:4; and see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 1:7).
one who removes. Takes the bread out of the oven.
this is permitted. And it is not like terumah since it does not absorb taste from the wine.
and barley bread is forbidden. It is to be treated as terumah.

because barley absorbs. It is the nature of barley to absorb more than wheat, and since the bread is hot it absorbs of the taste of the wine (for another law deriving from this see Hilchot Tum'at Okhlin 14:7).
an oven that he heated with cumin. He heated the oven for baking by burning terumah cumin (for example, terumah cumin that became impure).
and smell does not forbid. See Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 9:23, 15:33 and the rulings and opinions there.
even though its water was made foul. And their taste is noticeable in the water, but their taste spoils the water and ruins it.
they are permitted. The water may be used as unconsecrated.
for a taste that spoils does not forbid. A forbidden item whose taste passed into other food and spoiled its flavor does not forbid it (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 15:28).
it and its stalk. If it fell together with the stalk.

if the fenugreek seed alone has enough to impart taste to the wine etc.. And we do not consider the taste that passes from the stalk, since it is not customarily eaten and has no law of terumah, but only the seed (see above 2:4, 2:8).
and one of unconsecrated wine. And it does not have enough to nullify the terumah wine at one to a hundred.
he diluted each of them with water. He mixed each cup of wine with water to dilute it before drinking.

we regard the unconsecrated wine as if it were not there etc.. We do not consider the taste of the unconsecrated wine, but the taste of the terumah wine against all the water, and estimate whether the terumah wine has enough to impart taste to the water, according to the law of a kind mixed with a different kind (above 13:2; see also Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 16:31).

for we have already explained that water does not make the wine rise. That if the water by itself does not nullify the taste of the wine, the water does not combine with the unconsecrated wine to nullify the terumah wine at a hundred, as explained above 13:9, for their measures of nullification differ.
he rinses them. He washes the produce.
and they are permitted. Since they do not absorb from the terumah wine in this way.
he skims it. He removes the oil that floats on the wine.
fish brine. Liquid formed from pickling fish.
and he takes off a peel. He separates from the brine a layer the thickness of a peel, since the brine absorbs a little of the oil because of its strong taste (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 9:19).
he may not cook unconsecrated produce in it. Since it has absorbed the taste of the terumah and would release it into the unconsecrated dish.
and if he cooked, by imparting taste. If he transgressed and cooked, one checks whether the unconsecrated dish has a taste that came from the terumah, and if so it is treated as terumah.

and if he rinsed the pot with water or wine, it is permitted to cook in it. It does not require purging. Unlike other prohibitions where the pot must be purged to be made fit (see Hilchot Ma'akhalot Asurot 17:3 and Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 8:11-12), with terumah they were lenient (see Riko and Kesef Mishneh, who cited Maimonides' words to the sages of Lunel on this matter).
and terumah of the tithe. See above 3:20.
and challah. See Hilchot Bikkurim 5:13-14.
and first fruits. See ibid. 3:1-5.

and there is nothing requiring bringing to the place that is not specified in this verse, except for first fruits. All the things eaten only in Jerusalem are mentioned by name in this verse, except first fruits; hence the expression 'the terumah of your hand' mentioned in the verse refers to first fruits.
terumah of the tithe of demai. Produce about which it is doubtful whether it was tithed, and the Sages instituted that terumah of the tithe be separated from it out of doubt (Hilchot Ma'aser 9:1-2).
and so we have received. Thus it was received from earlier generations, although it has no source in the words of the Sages.
and we have regarded them. The priests.
even with challah of outside the Land. Even though its obligation outside the Land is mainly rabbinic (Hilchot Bikkurim 5:7).

for eating the holy things of the border is also like a service. Even what the priests eat outside Jerusalem is part of the service they were commanded to perform, and therefore a blessing over the commandment must be recited for it, in addition to the blessing of enjoyment over that food.
the service of a gift. Eating the priestly gifts is also part of the priests' service, just as eating the meat of offerings is a mitzvah (Hilchot Ma'aseh ha-Korbanot 10:1-2).
